value: Brazilian app for intercity bus travel: it pools travellers to charter executive buses, resells tickets from over 150 bus companies and now owns regulated bus lines.

Buser is a Brazilian app for intercity bus travel that has grown from a group-charter platform into a mix of three businesses: collaborative charter (fretamento colaborativo), regulated bus lines it now owns, and a marketplace that resells tickets from more than 150 bus companies. In the original model, travellers going to the same destination are pooled so that they split the cost of chartering an executive bus from a licensed charter company; Buser sells the seats, runs customer service, pricing, network planning and marketing, and does not own buses or employ drivers (the company's own pitch, and Valor Capital's description), taking a commission from the bus company (reported in 2019 at up to 35%, 20-25% on average). Trips can cost up to about 60% less than a bus-station ticket. Buses carry fatigue cameras and telemetry, and companies and drivers are certified by the transport regulator ANTT. It began when co-founder Marcelo Abritta, from Belo Horizonte, found it cheaper to charter a 48-seat bus for 30 relatives to his wedding in Bahia than to buy 30 tickets (November 2016). With his friend Marcelo Vasconcellos he launched a Facebook page on 2 June 2017, which had 10,000 followers in under 30 days; the first trip, planned for 7 July 2017, was blocked by a court order from incumbents, the passengers were refunded and the press coverage helped. The two founders then raised a seed from Canary, Yellow Ventures and Fundação Estudar Alumni Partners (early 2018), a Series A from Valor Capital, Monashees and Canary (end of 2018) and a Series B led by SoftBank's Latin America fund with Monashees, Valor, Canary and Grupo Globo (October 2019), which carried a plan to spend R$300 million in 12 months. After the pandemic it added a ticket marketplace (end of 2020), parcel delivery inside buses for companies (Buser Encomendas, May 2021), bus financing and urban transport plans, backed by a R$700 million Series C in June 2021 led by LGT Lightrock. It then built a WhatsApp sales channel (expected to reach 35% of revenue in 2022), relaunched its brand in 2024 and, per the press, passed US$100 million of annual revenue in 2024, with 20% growth in operating profit. In 2025 it raised R$30 million in media-for-equity from 4Equity Media Ventures to pay for marketing. In March 2026 it bought two regulated bus companies, Expresso JK and Transportes Santa Maria, its first acquisitions, and in November 2026 co-founder Marcelo Vasconcellos took over as CEO, with Abritta staying on. It reports gross revenue of R$580 million in 2025, expects R$700 million in 2026 and aims for R$1 billion by 2027 through acquisitions of traditional bus companies, AI and the marketplace; it has 14 million registered customers, carries about 5 million passengers a year and wants 6 million in 2027. The company still fights lawsuits from traditional operators and a federal prosecutor over whether its model needs ANTT authorisation, though a Federal Court in Espírito Santo declared the model legal in November 2024.

value: Problem: Brazil moves people by road. Valor Capital counted 4,600 destinations served by buses against 530 by air, and over 300 million bus tickets sold in 2019, twice as many as airline tickets. Yet most routes were run by one company under per-route government authorisations (about 65% of routes with a single operator in 2019), so prices were high and options poor, and many people turned to clandestine transport. Logic and why now: shared chartering lets an asset-light platform pool demand digitally and rent seats on buses that already exist, so a bus fills and costs fall. The model copies the logic of ride-hailing and of Flixbus in Germany, which grew an open market after deregulation (Valor's explanation). Minas Gerais authorising independent charter operators in 2021 and a favourable federal ruling in 2024 moved the regulatory risk in its favour, and Buser now buys licensed bus companies to put its pricing and data into them. Market size: NeoFeed (read, November 2026) cites the regulated road passenger market at R$15-20 billion a year and over 100 million passengers, 60% of which still happens offline. Buser itself reported R$580 million of gross revenue in 2025, so it is already about 3-4% of that market; a strong outcome could be 10-15% (R$2-3 billion), mostly through acquisition and marketplace. The sum is our own: R$15-20B x 10-15% = R$1.5-3B. What is different: it has the brand and the app that millions of Brazilians know, a regulatory track record, and technology (pricing, network planning, fatigue cameras) it can apply to acquired operators; competitors are traditional operators, ClickBus-style marketplaces and BlaBlaCar. Fit with Norte (our reading): this is a Fund I company (Norte's portfolio page), with founders who kept going through years of court battles; as a connector, Norte's role would be introducing top funds (the cap table shows SoftBank, Lightrock, Monashees, Valor) and operators. No source we read says when or in which round Norte invested. Risks: regulation and litigation (ANTT and prosecutors), bus safety incidents and legal responsibility for delays, margin pressure from owning operations, and execution of acquisitions. Travel demand is cyclical, as the pandemic showed.

value: Colombian electricity retailer for businesses that installs a smart meter and gives customers consumption analytics, a single invoice for all their sites and clean-energy options; it is also building distributed solar generation and an energy-software spin-off, Olibia.

Bia sells electricity to businesses in Colombia and wraps it in technology. It buys power in the wholesale market and resells it to companies, installing a smart meter (replacing the traditional one and handling the change of supplier) so the customer can see consumption by site and by hour, get alerts and forecasts, detect reactive-power problems, ask an AI assistant why consumption rose, centralise invoices for many sites in one payment, and see how much of its energy is clean (renewable-energy certificates are available at extra cost). Bia says its tariffs beat the grid operators' average for the same voltage level, and the pitch is that energy should be understood and chosen, not only paid. It was founded in 2022 in Bogotá by two ex-Rappi people, Juan Sebastián Ruales (CEO) and Guillermo Plaza, together with energy-sector executive Leonardo Velásquez. It launched with a US$6 million pre-seed in July 2022 led by Canary, with angels such as the Rappi founders and the founders of NotCo and Frubana. By October 2023, with a Series A of US$16.5 million led by Kaszek, it had more than 1,500 business clients; in November 2024, with a US$8.5 million bridge ahead of a Series B led by RA Capital's Planetary Health fund and IDB Lab, it reported more than 3,000 businesses (Coca-Cola Femsa and Falabella among them), 140 employees and more than US$8 million of monthly revenue, and said it had used up to US$20 million of debt facilities. In August 2026 it raised US$18.5 million led by Kaszek, with Endeavor Catalyst, RA Capital and the IDB, bringing total capital to about US$40 million, and reorganised as a group with three units: energy retail (more than 4,000 companies, including Coca-Cola, Falabella, Ikea and Parmalat, about 50 GWh a month, or roughly 0.7% of the national market), distributed generation (small hydro plants and 'remote panel' solar communities of 1 MW, aiming for at least 15 communities in 2026) and Olibia, a software spin-off of the operating system Bia built for its own acquisition, billing, collections and trading, in talks with customers in five countries and aimed at gas, water and telecoms as well as power. The CEO says the business will grow 60-70% in 2026 with 92% retention in the first cohort and an NPS of 83, and that it will open a free market-intelligence platform to the whole industry. Backers named in the press include Kaszek, Canary, Nazca, 8VC, Global Founders Capital, EWA Capital, WildSur, RA Capital, IDB Lab and Endeavor Catalyst; Norte Ventures appears in aggregator investor lists and in a 2026 LinkedIn event post that tags it, but no round article names it.

value: Problem: Colombian businesses buy electricity without seeing what they use until the bill arrives, with limited choice of supplier, and tariffs rose 15.3% a year between 2021 and 2024 (Corficolombiana, cited by Forbes Colombia), the sharpest rise in 23 years after a drought. A regulated or contract customer with several sites has no clean data, no forecast and no single invoice. Logic and why now: the market for larger customers is open to competition, so a retailer that buys well in the wholesale market (using hydrology and weather models) and installs its own smart meter can give a lower price and data at the same time. The meter and billing data are also a software asset, which Bia now spins off as Olibia. Rising prices and El Niño make customers receptive. Market size: Bia says 50 GWh a month is about 0.7% of the Colombian market (Ecosistema Startup, read), implying about 7,100 GWh a month or about 86 TWh a year nationally (our arithmetic: 50 / 0.007). At an assumed average of US$0.10-0.15 per kWh, that is about US$8-13 billion a year of electricity sales in Colombia; the part open to Bia's customers (businesses above the regulated threshold) is only a share of it (our assumption: 20-30%, so US$2-4 billion). Bia's own revenue run-rate of more than US$8 million a month (about US$100 million a year) is therefore roughly 2.5-5% of that addressable part, and a leader at 15-20% would be US$300-800 million, before Latin American expansion and software. What is different: the company combines a retail licence with its own meter, billing and trading software and reports 92% retention and an NPS of 83, which is uncommon for an energy supplier. A comparable the company itself names is Kraken Technologies, spun out of Octopus Energy, which in September 2025 reported US$500 million of contracted annualised revenue and more than 70 million accounts (Ecosistema Startup) - Bia's software unit is much earlier, with no licence revenue reported yet. Fit with Norte (our reading): ex-Rappi founders, a network of Latin American operators, and a cap table with Kaszek, Canary and Nazca fits Norte's co-investor role; the Manifesto says it brings top funds and operators into cap tables. No article says what Norte put in or when. Risks: wholesale-price exposure in a drought year (the CEO says demand is matched with contracts), regulatory change in Colombia's electricity market, financing needs for the energy contracts and solar communities (debt, guarantees), and the distraction of three business lines.

value: Brazilian fintech that gives manufacturers a co-branded Pix virtual card and an AI credit assistant so their small retail customers can buy in instalments while the manufacturer is paid upfront and Robbin carries the risk.

Robbin is a Brazilian fintech that lets manufacturers and distributors sell on credit to their small retail customers without carrying the credit risk. A large industry offers its retailers a co-branded virtual card (it sits in a digital wallet app and runs on Pix instead of the Visa or Mastercard networks); the retailer buys in instalments from the industry's suppliers and earns points (convertible into discounts on future purchases or Livelo points), and the industry receives the money upfront while Robbin takes over the collection. Robbin builds and runs the whole credit journey: customer onboarding with automatic validation and fraud detection, credit intelligence and limits, risk management and capital. Its AI sales assistant, Robbinson, runs on WhatsApp, the channel the sales team already uses, and approves credit in real time during the sales conversation (the site claims decisions in 30 seconds instead of two weeks, and that a network buys 73% more; these are company claims). It sells to textile, construction materials, electronics, auto parts, food, pharma, household goods, telecom and marketplace players, and also offers its AI agents (KYC and anti-money-laundering checks in about 20 seconds, credit, monitoring and collection) to banks, insurers and asset managers. It was founded in 2023 (about two and a half years before May 2026) by Leonardo Moura (CEO; about 15 years at XP, where he built the international debt-capital-markets franchise, and at Itaú BBA in London and New York), Henrique Meyer (COO; Itaú BBA, Citi and HSBC debt markets) and Tomás Corrêa (CTO; co-founder and CTO of OpenCo, the digital lender formed by the merger of Geru and Rebel with SoftBank backing, where he led technology for almost ten years). The founders' thesis is that retailers got modern card and instalment experiences while the link between industry and retail was left with short, rigid terms and badly calibrated limits. In May 2026 it announced its first institutional round, a US$8 million seed co-led by Canary, Atlântico and Caravela, with AB Seed, Norte Ventures, Clocktower and Tomorrow Capital, plus a US$100 million receivables fund (FIDC) structured with Augme, the XP manager, to fund the credit it extends (it plans to deploy all of it by the end of 2027). Until then its funding was bilateral lines from banks, which had financed about R$200 million of credit since inception. It had eight partner industries (Cantu Pneus, Chilli Beans, Baterias Moura, Malwee, Brinox, Votorantim, Tigre and Gerdau's Juntos Somos Mais marketplace among them), a potential base of more than 300,000 small and mid-sized businesses linked to them, a target of 50 industries by the end of 2026, and a default rate it says is below the 5.5% Brazilian-central-bank SME average. It targets industries with annual revenue above R$500 million.

value: Problem: a manufacturer selling to thousands of small retailers has to decide, for each one, whether to give credit, how much and for how long. Short, rigid terms and badly calibrated limits cap its sales, and the retailer has no access to the instalment and benefits experience a consumer gets. Banks serve these small companies badly, and the industry carries the credit risk and the collection effort on its balance sheet. Logic and why now: Pix gives a cheap real-time payment rail, so a card-like product does not need card networks; AI agents make onboarding, fraud checks, limit setting and collection cheap enough for small tickets; and a receivables fund (FIDC) lets the company fund credit without using its own equity. The industry gets cash upfront, the retailer gets terms, and Robbin earns on the transaction and the credit spread. Market size: no published figure for B2B trade credit in Brazil was found (search results gave only default statistics). Our bottom-up estimate: the company says its eight partner industries give access to more than 300,000 small and mid-sized businesses. If each bought R$50-150 thousand a year on instalment terms (our assumption), that is R$15-45 billion of annual purchases from only the current partners; at an assumed 2-4% revenue per real financed (fees and credit spread), the revenue pool is R$0.3-1.8 billion a year from them alone. With 50 industries (the company's end-2026 goal) the pool could be several times that. A strong outcome of, say, 10-20% of such a pool would be several hundred million reais of revenue. What is different: it combines a co-branded Pix card owned by each industry, AI agents in WhatsApp and a fund that carries the risk, run by founders from debt capital markets and from a digital lender. Comparables (SME trade-credit fintechs and card issuers) were not researched. Fit with Norte (our reading): obsessed, experienced founders at the earliest institutional stage, with credit and technology experience, which matches a follower role in a seed led by Canary, Atlântico and Caravela; Norte's network of operators and industry executives can open doors to large manufacturers, the customers the model depends on. Risks: credit losses and funding cost if the portfolio grows faster than risk models learn (a thin loss history, a young company); dependence on a few large industries; competition from banks and trade-credit fintechs; and the need for repeated FIDC capacity.
note: No published market size for B2B trade credit in Brazil was found (a search returned only Serasa blog and Forbes default statistics, not used). Our bottom-up: 300,000 linked SMEs (company claim, Finsiders) x R$50-150k yearly purchases (assumption) = R$15-45B; x 2-4% revenue yield (assumption) = R$0.3-1.8B. value: Brazilian technology-skills school that began as an income-share developer bootcamp and now sells AI courses, workshops and corporate training, including a programme for lawyers with OAB state sections.

Trybe is a Brazilian school for technology skills that began by training software developers and is now centred on teaching artificial intelligence at work. In its first form, a developer course of about 12 months (later also mobile, data science, cybersecurity and data engineering) could be paid only after the graduate got a job above a salary floor: the student paid up to 17% of the salary, over up to five years, for a total of R$36,000 (the company calls it the shared-success model, MSC; the press calls it an income share agreement, ISA). Trybe made money from those instalments and from deals with employers who hired graduates; 94% of graduates were working within 30 days of graduating (company claim, 2021). It built a financing arm, Trybe SCD, authorised by the Central Bank as a direct credit company in May 2021, and raised a R$50 million receivables fund (FIDC) in March 2021 to fund the ISA. It was founded in August 2019 by five partners who earlier built AppProva, an education-data startup with 5 million students that was sold to Somos Educação: Matheus Goyas (CEO), Cláudio Lensing, João Daniel Duarte, Marcos Moura and Rafael Torres. Six months after opening it raised a R$42 million Series A led by Atlantico (about US$10 million), with Norte among the investors, then a US$6 million extension led by Base Partners in January 2021, the acquisition of the Santa Catarina software house Jungle Devs in June 2021 and a R$145 million (US$27 million) Series B in October 2021 led by Base Partners and Untitled, at a valuation of about R$1.3 billion. By then it had 2,200 students, 130 partner companies (CI&T, Ford, Localiza, Méliuz, Thoughtworks, XP), more than 190,000 applications and students in eight countries besides Brazil. When tech hiring turned in 2022, Trybe cut 47 people (about 10% of nearly 500) in August 2022 and 128 people (about 35% of staff) in June 2023, saying it aimed at breakeven within 180 days; it launched an intensive live course (FIT) and a free JavaScript course for 2,000 people to bring in students. Its public site today sells AI courses, workshops and training for companies and for lawyers: it says more than 1,000 companies have developed their teams with it, that it is the AI-training partner of 16 OAB state sections, and that its AI-literacy programme for law, run with the OAB sections, Jusbrasil and ITS Rio, has had more than 100,000 professionals. The date of the move to AI training is not given in the sources read; no round after 2021 was found.

value: Problem: Brazil's tech sector cannot find enough trained people: Brasscom projected demand of 797,000 professionals from 2021 to 2025 against 53,000 graduates a year in technology courses, a gap of 106,000 a year (Convergência Digital, December 2021). Many candidates cannot pay for a bootcamp up front. Now a second gap has opened, in using AI at work: employees and professional groups such as lawyers need practical training at speed, because the tools change weekly. Logic and why now: the income-share model aligns the school with the student's job outcome and made it attractive to investors in 2020-21, when hiring was strong; the 2022-23 downturn showed its weakness (graduates take longer to place, financing needs are large). The new AI-training line moves to a lighter model (subscriptions, workshops, corporate training) that sells to employers and professional associations with a distribution channel, the OAB, and does not carry student credit. Market size: we found no published figure for the market of corporate AI training in Brazil. Our bottom-up estimate for lawyers: Brazil has on the order of one million registered lawyers (our assumption, not read), so an annual subscription of R$1,000-2,000 (assumption) would give a pool of R$1-2 billion; a 5-10% share is R$50-200 million. For company training, the company says it has served over 1,000 companies; at R$30,000-100,000 per contract (assumption) and 300-500 contracts a year, revenue would be R$10-50 million. These are our assumptions only. What is different: it has a large Brazilian base of developers' alumni and employer relationships, a brand known by 190,000 applicants, and an association channel (OAB) that lowers the cost of acquiring customers; it also has experience of running credit for students. Fit with Norte (our reading): Norte invested at the Series A when the founders were second-time entrepreneurs with a sold company (AppProva) and a clear talent-supply problem; Norte's network of operators who hire developers fits the early distribution need. Risks: the 2023 layoffs show a dependence on tech hiring; the AI-training market is crowded (universities, platforms, vendors) and low-priced; the pivot is recent and little is published on its revenue; the finance arm's loan book from 2020-22 may still weigh on results.

value: Brazilian payment orchestrator for physical stores: one integration connects a shop's point-of-sale software to every acquirer and Pix provider and routes each transaction by lowest cost.

Destaxa is a Brazilian payments company that sits between a shop's point-of-sale (PDV) software and the card machines and payment processors, so one integration lets a retailer use any acquirer or Pix provider and route each transaction through the cheapest option. It describes itself as the first payment orchestrator for physical (offline) merchants and says it will never be a payment processor, only infrastructure, which keeps it neutral between acquirers. Its customers are the software houses and commercial-automation vendors that build PDV systems (it was connected to about 130 of them in 2024, with nearly 150,000 PDV clients, of which fewer than 5,000 were Destaxa's), and through them the merchants, with monthly revenue of R$100,000 to R$1 million. Products on its site: a TEF (card-payment integration) and an advanced version, the DTX+ web platform to set parameters for every client in real time, a card-and-Pix integration for Android smart terminals (it bets on the 'androidisation' of the PDV market, where each acquirer's Android machine forces vendors to maintain a separate integration), an 'Oferta Inteligente' programme that lets automation vendors earn a share of their clients' card transactions, receivables advance (the cheapest working capital a merchant has) and a partnership to sell energy directly from the producer with savings of up to 30%. Earlier it sold a merchant-side dashboard with reconciliation of cards and banks, fee audits and cash-flow automation. It was founded in 2021 by Felipe Ayres, a third-time entrepreneur (he earlier created the asset manager F3 Capital and the sub-acquirer Nexu), together with businessman Sigvard Von Baranow Neto. Ayres got the idea of orchestration after a trip to India to study UPI, where he met a former sub-acquirer who had moved to orchestration. Growth in new clients per month went from 5-20 in 2022 to 50-100 in 2023 and 300-500 in 2024, with a target of 5,000 a month by mid-2025. Processing reached more than R$2 billion a year at the end of 2023 and about R$4 billion a year in mid-2024; in June 2024 it was testing its platform as infrastructure for acquirers (one in test, one in talks). Backers named in the press are Quona Capital (lead of the 2022 seed), Caravela, Norte Ventures, the angels Tiago Dalvi (Olist) and Alessio Alionço (Pipefy), and, in the November 2023 R$30 million round, Astella (lead), Supera, Quona, Caravela and Endeavor ScaleUp Ventures. The CEO said in June 2024 that a Series A was planned for early 2025; the sources read do not show that it happened, and no later news was found.

value: Problem: a small merchant sells with many card machines and contracts, does not know which acquirer is cheapest for each transaction, and cannot easily renegotiate. The software house that makes its point-of-sale system must build and maintain a separate integration for each acquirer, a growing burden as Android terminals multiply. Logic and why now: Pix and the open card market gave merchants choice, and Android machines made it possible to run one payment app on any acquirer's terminal. An orchestrator that is neutral and cheap to integrate can give the software house new revenue (a share of each transaction) and the merchant the lowest-cost route per transaction. Market size: Abecs reports R$4.5 trillion of card volume in Brazil in 2025 (Finsiders, read), with online purchases above R$1 trillion, leaving roughly R$3.4 trillion in physical stores (our subtraction: 4.5 - 1.0 and a little). Destaxa processes about R$4 billion a year (2024, company), about 0.1% of the in-store volume. If it reached 5% of in-store volume (about R$170 billion) and kept a net take of 0.05-0.15% of volume (our assumption: a fraction of the spread it helps save, shared with the PDV vendor), revenue would be R$85-255 million. A strong outcome is therefore in the low hundreds of millions of reais of revenue. What is different: neutrality (never a processor), integration with about 130 PDV vendors (distribution, not direct sales), and a revenue share for the vendor. Online orchestrators (Yuno, Malga, PoolPay) and the offline player Shipay are named as comparables by Finsiders. Fit with Norte (our reading): a serial founder with a payments background and an infrastructure-style product, at the seed stage with Quona and Caravela leading; Norte joined as follower in 2022 and can help with introductions to PDV vendors, acquirers and later funds. Risks: acquirers may cut costs for vendors directly or build their own multi-acquirer terminals; low take rate per transaction; concentration in the PDV vendors' channel; and no published sign of growth or a Series A since mid-2024.

AI sales agents on WhatsApp that answer, qualify and book the leads generated by a company's ads, tie each sale back to the ad that started it and charge per qualified meeting.

Patagon AI sells AI agents that talk to the people who answer a company's ads. A lead who clicks an ad on Meta or another channel lands in a WhatsApp conversation instead of a web form; the agent replies in under a minute, at any hour, holds an open conversation (the buyer can ask anything or send audio, unlike a chatbot built as a decision tree), qualifies the lead by the client's own rules, books the meeting or showroom visit with a human seller and keeps following up until the person answers or opts out. The second layer is attribution: it captures the ad click and campaign data at first touch, ties it to every conversation and sends the outcome (qualified, booked, sold) back to the ad platforms and the CRM as an offline conversion, so the client sees which ad brought which buyer and campaigns optimise for buyers instead of clicks. Its site now also offers to run the ads themselves, as an end-to-end marketing service for sectors such as automotive, education, finance, real estate, insurance, retail, health, telecoms and travel, and integrates with Salesforce, Meta and Microsoft tools. It makes money on results rather than seats: the client pays a fixed fee when a conversation ends in a meeting with a human seller (about R$50 in Brazil as of November 2025), on top of a setup fee of about R$10,000 and a minimum monthly fee that suited large companies but kept small ones out. The company promises about 30% more qualified leads. A Mitsubishi operation in Ecuador is the showcase: 35% more sales with a 20% smaller marketing budget, as told by the company. The company was founded in 2023 in Argentina by four people, two Ecuadorians and two Argentines: David Grandes (CEO), Mariano Rey (CMO), Cristian Adamo (CTO) and Roberto Guerrero (CRO). Grandes had co-founded ZAK, a Brazilian restaurant-software startup backed by Tiger Global and Monashees that was later shut down, and had worked at OLX and Restorando; Rey says the product is what he needed as head of marketing at Botmaker and head of growth at NaranjaX. Traction: a US$1.1 million pre-seed in late 2024 (OneVC and 17Sigma) paid for the Colombian launch; the company aimed at US$130,000 of annual recurring revenue at the end of 2024 and reported US$1 million in October 2025. It entered Brazil in April 2025, which became its second market by revenue after Ecuador; by November 2025 it had more than 100 clients in 12 to 15 countries (30 in Brazil, among them Pluxee, with banks and tech unicorns in implementation, a process of three to six months) and a team of about 25 in Argentina and Brazil. In November 2025 it raised R$15 million (about US$2.7 million) led by Kfund, with all earlier investors including Norte Ventures following, to build a self-onboarding product that lets small companies start without a sales process. Its target for 2025 was about US$2 million in revenue.

value: Problem: companies that buy ads to generate leads lose most of the value between the click and the sale. A form is answered hours later by an overloaded team, nobody can tell good leads from noise, and the ad budget cannot be tied to sales. In Latin America the natural channel is WhatsApp, and the usual answer, a chatbot built as a decision tree, is rigid. Logic and why now: language models make an open conversation possible at a cost that lets the company charge per qualified meeting instead of per seat, and WhatsApp is the default channel for consumer-to-business talk in the region (Kfund cites hundreds of millions of users). Linking each conversation to the ad click and sending the result back to the ad platform closes the loop that marketing teams lack, so the product sells ROI, not software. Market: no published market size for AI sales agents on WhatsApp in Latin America was found. A bottom-up estimate: Brazil Journal gives a price of about R$50 per qualified conversation. If 5,000 mid-sized and large advertisers in the region (our assumption) each generated 2,000 qualified conversations a year (assumption), the revenue pool is about R$500 million (US$90 million) a year; at 20,000 advertisers and 3,000 conversations it is about R$3 billion. A realistic strong outcome is a 5-10% share, or tens of millions of dollars of revenue, far above the US$1 million ARR of October 2025. What is different: pay-for-outcome pricing, attribution built into the agent, and a regional focus (bilingual agents, local messaging habits, teams in Argentina and Brazil). Competitors named in the press are chatbot vendors such as Blip, which is adding AI layers; global conversation platforms were not researched. Fit with Norte (our reading, from the Manifesto read 2026-11-24): obsessed, experienced founders, one of them a repeat founder with Brazilian experience; Norte joined as a follower in a round led by a European fund, and its network of Brazilian operators can open large Brazilian accounts, where the company has 30 clients and its largest implementation backlog. Risks: low switching costs and fast-moving model vendors; dependence on Meta's WhatsApp policies and prices; a pay-per-meeting model that exposes the company to the client's lead quality; and revenue concentration in Ecuador and a few big clients.

value: Brazilian private B2B marketplace where large brands sell surplus inventory to vetted small and mid-sized retailers, with AI matching and pricing and a 12% take rate.

BackChannel is a private B2B marketplace in Brazil where large brands sell their excess inventory to vetted small and mid-sized retailers. A brand lists a lot, sets the rules for who may buy it (for example, only offline stores far from big cities, so the cheap stock does not undercut its own online collection), and the platform matches the lot with buyers that fit, using AI for matching and dynamic pricing. The buyer sees a chat-style interface in which they describe their business and receive recommended lots. BackChannel does not hold or manage the goods; it earns a take rate of about 10% to 12% of each transaction (12% in March 2026), with an average ticket of about R$50,000, plus a logistics fee paid by the buyer in the first model. It was started by two Argentines, Guillermo Freire (CEO) and Guillermo Arslanian, who had founded Trocafone ten years earlier, a used-phone e-commerce that reached about R$400 million of yearly revenue in Brazil. Working with Apple, Samsung and Motorola, they saw how every new model left old stock in the channel, creating channel conflict and cash tied up in inventory; they found no Brazilian solution but found Ghost, a US private marketplace for brand overstock, and adapted the model to Latin America. They left the day-to-day of Trocafone (where they remain partners) in 2024 to start it. The founders say the company was built with AI from the start: the platform was built in two months, and by March 2026 it had a team of about 40 and eight AI agents handling prospecting, emails and onboarding. Traction: a R$17 million pre-seed in October 2024, led by Cathay Latam (an investor in Ghost), financed the first product. By June 2025 it had 30 brand sellers, more than 1.5 million items listed and 50 vetted buyers. It closed 2025, its first full year, with about R$25 million of gross merchandise value (GMV), growing about 30% a month according to the company; by March 2026 it reported about 100 large brands and 18,000 retailer buyers (a smaller figure of over 1,000 active buyers appears in the funding release). Fashion and footwear came first, because the ten largest fashion brands hold most of the market and R$30 to 40 million each in idle stock; cosmetics followed. In March 2026 it raised a R$25 million seed led by Sunna Ventures with nine other funds including Norte Ventures. The plan is to speed up the onboarding of sellers and buyers with agents, add categories such as beauty, personal care, electronics and food, import surplus from China, the US and Europe, and launch embedded finance (buy-now-pay-later and payment terms) for retailers. The company aims at R$150 million of GMV in 2026 and R$1 billion within three years.

value: Problem: brands that launch new collections or models are left with millions of reais of unsold stock. It ties up cash, loses value each month and, if sold in the usual way, leaks into the brand's own online channel or ends up in informal markets such as Brás with no control over where it goes. Small retailers, on the other side, cannot buy branded goods at good prices and often lack credit to do so. Logic and why now: a private marketplace lets the brand set who can buy and where, which protects its prices, while AI handles matching, pricing and the prospecting that once needed a large sales team (the founders say the platform was built in two months, against six months and twice the staff at Trocafone). The same founders already ran a large two-sided marketplace in Brazil, so they know how to find liquidity on both sides. Market: Freire puts the addressable market at US$9 billion in Brazil (company claim, Brazil Journal) and US$8-9 billion in the first verticals (Startups.com.br); an independent figure is Abrappe's survey of retail losses, R$35 billion in 2023 and a forecast R$36.5 billion in 2025, quoted in a Startups.com.br opinion article (read; not all of it is overstock). Our own check: if 100 brands each place R$30 million of stock a year through the platform (assumption), GMV is R$3 billion and a 12% take rate yields about R$360 million of revenue; the company's own goal of R$1 billion of GMV would give about R$120 million. What is different: it is the first, as far as the founders found, to bring the Ghost model to Brazil, it controls the channel through rules set by the seller, and it plans to add credit for the small buyer, which would raise the take per transaction. Ghost (about US$100 million raised, Startups.com.br) is a foreign comparable, not a competitor in Brazil. Fit with Norte (our reading, from the Manifesto read 2026-11-24): repeat founders who already built a marketplace and have the network that Norte values; Norte entered at the pre-seed and followed in the seed, a follower role next to funds such as Cathay Latam and Sunna. Risks: liquidity on both sides of a marketplace, brands going direct or to rival liquidators, a lumpy GMV that depends on a few large sellers, the credit product exposing the company to default, and results that are the company's own figures from a business only a year and a half old.

value: Igual is a legal-technology company from Curitiba that builds software for digital law firms working on labor law (trabalhista) that aims to bring labor law to the people who need it most. Its site says it uses technology and AI so that lawyers can serve more people better, and describes three layers: legal software that runs a firm's case flow end to end, AI applied across the legal journey to automate repetitive tasks and speed up decisions while keeping a human lawyer in the loop, and tools that let a firm generate qualified demand, offer end-to-end service and use a settlement (conciliation) framework meant to shorten the life cycle of a case. Stanford's CodeX TechIndex classifies it as matter-management software for litigation, sold to law firms on a subscription, and says small operational teams can coordinate large volumes of lawsuits with it. The company was founded in 2024 and is based in Curitiba; its job posts as of November 2026 (a commercial analyst, a systems analyst working with Python and Odoo, an infrastructure analyst) show a team that is still building its commercial and internal systems. Investor directories list Norte Ventures in a 2024 pre-seed and a later seed of about US$2 million with BFF Ventures, Honey Island Capital, 1616 Ventures and 4UM Investments, but no article or company page that was readable states these rounds, so none is recorded. The founders are three people from Curitiba's technology scene (their LinkedIn profiles, read through Linked API in November 2026): André Boaventura, co-founder and CEO, who was EBANX's chief marketing officer until 2022; Ariel Patschiki, co-founder and CTO, who was EBANX's chief product officer until 2023 after a decade in its product teams; and the lawyer Jacqueline Jianoti, co-founder, who came from the legal and institutional-relations side of the accounting platform Contabilizei and still runs her own law practice. Their profiles date their work at Igual from January to March 2024. No customers, revenue or volume figures were found in readable public sources, so this profile stays short.

value: Problem: workers with modest incomes often have valid labor claims but are not served by traditional firms, which find small cases unprofitable; digital labor-law firms try to serve them at volume but are short of tools to manage thousands of cases, to find clients and to settle quickly. value: Brazilian insurer (Susep-authorised) that designs and underwrites embedded insurance for fintechs, lenders, retailers and platforms, connected by one API.

180° Insurance (180 Seguros) is a Brazilian insurance company, authorised by Susep, that builds and underwrites insurance products for other companies to sell inside their own customer journeys. A fintech, digital bank, lender, retailer, real-estate platform or cooperative connects through a single API, and 180 designs the product with it (white label or co-branded), runs issuance, claims and commission splits automatically, and gives the partner a hub with metrics, quotes, policies and claims. The partner earns a commission and a recurring revenue line, 180 earns a fee on each policy sold (its early description was a success fee) and, as it became a carrier, the underwriting result. Its largest product today is credit-life (prestamista) insurance sold with loans, followed by life, Pix and extended-warranty cover, home, business and personal-accident policies; a phone-insurance product was next in 2025. Partners named in the press include Loft, Caju, Buser, Zul+, Mottu, iClinic, Pipo Saúde, DMCard, CredPago, Solfácil and QI Tech. It was founded in October 2020 in São Paulo by two Nubank alumni, Mauro Levi D'Ancona (CEO, who ran fundraising and investor relations at Nubank) and Franco Lamping (a software engineer, later CTO), with Alex Körner, an insurance executive from Mapfre and Santander, who has since left to found Dobbra.ai. They saw that Brazilian insurance was little digital and little penetrated, that Susep had opened a regulatory innovation agenda, and that insurance could be sold at the moment of purchase. It reached the market in April 2021 with a R$44 million seed, the largest for insurance in Latin America at the time and the first seed in Brazil for Dragoneer and Rainfall. Traction: at the end of 2021 it had eight clients; in February 2022, nine products across eight channels and 50 employees, including an hourly R$0.49 cover for items left in cars sold with the Zul+ blue-zone parking app, called the first intermittent insurance in Latin America. The R$177 million Series A of February 2022 financed hiring (to about 110) and joint ventures with large partners. Growth later was fast: annualised revenue of about R$100 million in December 2024, R$384 million in May 2025 and a run rate of R$348 million to R$500 million expected at the end of 2025, with growth of about 500% in 2025, according to the company. More than 80% of claims are analysed and settled by its own models. In September 2025 it raised R$50 million in a pre-Series B (R$35 million of equity and R$15 million of subordinated debt that counts toward Susep's regulatory capital) at a valuation of R$1.35 billion, and in October 2025 Vivo Ventures added US$2.5 million to build insurance products for Vivo's customers. Next, the company is building an AI vertical: a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server through which partners' AI agents quote, sell and service policies with no custom integration (it announced a partnership with Klubi's agent). The CEO said he wanted a Series B of at least US$50 million in the first half of 2026; none was found by November 2026.

Banks, fintechs, retailers and platforms that own the customer relationship and the purchase moment do not have insurance products designed for their journey, nor the licence, the actuarial and claims machinery and the integrations with insurers. Logic and why now: embedded insurance sold at checkout converts better and costs less to acquire, Pix and open-finance rails put more digital credit and payments in the hands of platforms, and Susep's regulatory sandbox and innovation agenda let a technology company become a carrier. 180 sells to partners that already have the customers, shares commission with them and, as it grew, took the risk itself. A realistic share: with a revenue run rate around R$350 to 500 million in 2025, 1% of a premium pool of R$300 billion would already be R$3 billion; our assumption is that a leading embedded carrier could reach 1-2% of premiums in the long run, which means R$3-6 billion, an order of magnitude above today's size. What is different: it is a carrier plus a technology platform, with product design per partner; the CEO says no other startup competes in the mass segment, with Pier, Justo and Darwin focused on auto through brokers (Brazil Journal, 2025); incumbents such as Mapfre, Zurich and Tokio Marine are the real competitors. value: Online school for tech and AI careers across Latin America that began with no-upfront-cost bootcamps (pay after getting a job) and now also sells AI talent and training to companies.

Henry (HENRY, short for "high earner, not rich yet") is an online school that trains Latin Americans to work in technology and connects them with employers. Its original offer, launched in March 2020, was a full-time bootcamp of about four months (or eight months part time) in full-stack development and data science, with no upfront cost: the student paid only after getting a job, through an income-share agreement of 15% of salary for two years capped at US$4,000. The company says most graduates find a tech job within six months and multiply their previous pay several times. Today the site sells AI-focused careers (Full Stack + AI, AI engineering, AI automation, data science and a new part-time Forward Deployed Engineer programme) with payment plans, and a business side: AI Talent (hiring graduates with no intermediary fees), AI Training for company teams, Henry Projects (graduates work on a client's backlog at no cost), live sessions and Henry Data, an educational analytics offer. The idea came to Martín Borchardt, an Argentine serial entrepreneur, after he saw half of his developers at the payments startup Nubi resign for dollar-paying jobs in 2018, when the peso collapsed. After a first attempt at student loans for existing academies failed with devaluation, he designed a school that trains people from zero and shares the risk. He founded Henry with his sister Luz Borchardt (acquisition) and with Leonardo Maglia, Federico Hernández and Manuel Barna, started in the Summer 2020 batch of Y Combinator (after being turned down in 2018), and has run the company as a remote-first team with no offices. Traction: 800 students by December 2020, with 200 graduates and 600 students in Colombia, Chile, Uruguay and Argentina by the end of that year, and about 30% of students in Colombia in January 2021. A US$1.5 million seed (December 2020) was followed by a US$10 million Series A in May 2022 led by Kayyak Ventures and Seaya Cathay Latam. By then it had 2,500 graduates, 5,000 students in training, 25,000 applications a month, 1,500 employers, about 105 staff and a target of 100,000 trained developers and breakeven in 2023. The YC page lists a team of about 100. Students come from Argentina (50%), Colombia (25%) and Mexico (15%), with Mexico and Colombia the priority markets. The 2025 target of 100,000 graduates was not reported as met, and no revenue figures after 2022 were found.

Accion's 2020 release said, from Henry's own estimate, more than a million engineering vacancies in the region against fewer than 100,000 trained professionals. Logic and why now: an income-share model aligns the school with the outcome (it only earns if the graduate gets paid), remote work and the dollar-paying demand of foreign employers created high wages for graduates, and online cohorts have almost no marginal cost. The AI wave moved the offer to AI engineering and a business side that sells talent and training to companies. Market: no independent market size for LatAm tech bootcamps was read. Bottom-up: the company's goal was 100,000 graduates; at a maximum of US$4,000 each that is up to US$400 million of lifetime revenue over several years, and at a realistic 20,000 paying graduates a year and an average of US$2,500 collected (assumptions) the annual pool is about US$50 million; corporate training and hiring fees could add a similar order. A strong outcome would be a leading regional position with tens of millions of dollars of annual revenue. What is different: zero upfront cost and a graduate-pays-later model with no debt, remote cohorts with a career coach and employer network, and a quick pivot to AI careers. Competitors named in the press: Microverse (also YC, ISAs), Platzi, Acamica, Crehana and Protalento (Forbes Colombia). Fit with Norte (our reading, from the Manifesto read 2026-11-24): a repeat founder from the Nubi exit with a strong team and a mission of upward mobility; value that a network of operators gives is access to employers and later-stage funds. The sources do not show Norte in any round, so its exact role is not recorded. Risks: income-share economics depend on graduates getting hired and paying, which weakens when tech hiring falls and AI tools lower entry-level demand; ISA financing needs capital; the 2025 goal was missed or not reported; and the company's later revenue and financing were not found.

value: Brazilian HR-tech that digitises occupational health and safety: online booking and tracking of exams, reports and legal programmes, with eSocial filing; acquired by Senior Sistemas in 2026.

Salú is a Brazilian HR-tech company that digitises occupational health and safety, the legal chain of exams and paperwork that every employer must run for its workers. In the traditional process a new hire had to find a clinic, book by phone or email, take the exam in person and bring the result to the employer, while HR acted as go-between and then typed the data into the government system (eSocial). Salú's SaaS platform lets the employee book exams online, tracks the whole life cycle (admission, periodic and dismissal exams, reports, ASOs, risk and medical-control programmes, certificates, leaves, absenteeism, protective equipment) and sends the obligations to eSocial, backed by an operations team and an accredited network of clinics; companies can also hire an on-site doctor or run a corporate clinic managed by Salú. It charges a monthly fee per covered life that varies with the modules used. It was founded in 2020 in São Paulo by René Neme (CEO), André Boff and Ricardo Silveira, with the physician Irineu Massaia. The founders' view in 2022 was that occupational health is a captive, provider-centred market, protected by law, and that Salú had to invert the logic and serve HR; the cheap entry point of exams was meant to become a "one-stop shop" for company health, with a chronic-care tool and a health-plan history viewer already added. Traction: about 100 to 108 clients and more than 30,000 lives by early 2022 (C6, Olist, Loft, Viveo, GetNinjas, RD Station, Warren), a target of 120,000 lives by the end of that year, and a team of about 50. In March 2022 it raised R$12 million, its first and only disclosed round, led by SoftBank's Latin America fund, and in September hired Sergio Cagno as chief medical officer. By 2025 it reported net revenue of R$76.8 million, annual recurring revenue of R$97.2 million, an adjusted EBITDA margin of 20.2%, more than 800 clients in every state (Nubank, XP, QuintoAndar, GPA, C6 Bank, Afya, Ipiranga), more than a million appointments, about 300,000 hours given back to HR teams and about 250 employees; revenue grew 115.5% a year from 2023 to 2025. On 10 June 2026 Senior Sistemas, a Brazilian HR and ERP software group, agreed to buy 100% of Salú for R$318.7 million (about 3.5 times last-12-month revenue of about R$100 million), its largest purchase and its first in health, to add occupational health to its human-capital suite just as the NR-1 rule on workplace risk management comes into force. The deal required approval by the competition authority Cade, and René Neme stays at the helm. The company registry shows Senior's executives as administrators from September 2026, which suggests the deal closed by then.

value: Problem: every Brazilian employer is legally obliged to run occupational health and safety programmes and exams for each worker, but the market is fragmented, manual and provider-centred: clinics set the rules, HR chases paper and employees lose days. Compliance errors expose companies to fines and lawsuits. Logic and why now: a software layer that books, tracks and files each obligation lowers the cost of compliance, and the rule is mandatory, so demand does not depend on a discretionary budget. Digital eSocial reporting and the arrival of the NR-1 risk-management rule (Senior calls it the trigger) make a unified data trail more valuable. Market: no published market size for Brazilian occupational health was read. Bottom-up, with assumptions: about 45 million formal employees (assumption, to be checked against IBGE) each needing about one exam or programme service a year at an average of R$100-200 (assumption) is a pool of R$4.5-9 billion a year, of which the software and operations margin could be a fraction. The best evidence of value is the market's own: a strategic buyer paid R$318.7 million, about 3.5 times revenue, for a company with R$76.8 million of 2025 revenue and 20% EBITDA margin; the Senior platforms alone manage more than 11 million workers. What is different: it combines software with a service operation, uses occupational health as a low-cost way into the HR budget, and grew above 100% a year while profitable. Competitors in occupational-health software and clinic networks were not researched. Fit with Norte (our reading, from the Manifesto read 2026-11-24): founders who focused on a mandatory process with a clear buyer and brought SoftBank, Aggir, Tau and health-sector angels to the cap table in the first institutional round, with Norte as a follower; the outcome shows that the follower role can still return capital in a few years. Norte's return on its stake is not public. Risks: price pressure from clinics and large insurers, regulatory change, dependence on the clinic network's quality, and integration under a new owner.

value: Software that digitises the operations of private credit in Latin America: asset onboarding, collateral verification, servicing and reporting for lenders and borrowers of asset-backed debt.

Vaas builds the operating software of private credit in Latin America: the back office that lenders, fintech borrowers and servicers use to onboard assets, verify collateral and run a debt facility day to day. A fintech that borrows against a portfolio of loans, devices or receivables normally reports to its lenders in spreadsheets and email, and every facility goes through a queue of manual checks. Vaas replaces that with one platform: a loan-tape mapper that turns a borrower's data into the lender's format, daily document verification with an OCR and AI engine, digital signature, ownership and payment tracking, waiver portals and reporting for originators, lenders, servicers and securitisation vehicles. The company says it began as a direct servicing tool and has become an embedded infrastructure platform, and that it now grows by servicing the assets directly and by tokenising assets. It sells to companies on both sides of the loan, with pricing that the sources do not give. It was founded in 2022 by Valentina Valencia, from Cali, Colombia, who started at PayJoy in 2016 and then worked at Architect Capital, one of the first debt funds to structure credit facilities for Latin American startups, so she saw both borrowers and lenders struggle with structured debt. She raised a US$5 million seed, led by a16z, in February 2023 when the team had 32 people (many from Globant, Mercado Libre and Rappi) and two clients, and says she landed a16z before having a product. Traction as the company tells it: first clients Addi and PayJoy; Goldman Sachs and Architect adopted it as lenders and later named it a verification agent; a first Mexican deal with Clara and Goldman Sachs; digital signature adopted by Bancolombia and Actinver; a waiver portal for CIM; and daily document verification for all clients. It operates in Colombia and Mexico. It won the Latin American final of She Loves Tech in September 2023, and Valencia made Forbes' 30 Under 30 list in 2025. 30N Ventures published why it invested in Vaas, describing it as the operating backbone of asset-backed lending; the size and date of that investment were not found.

value: Problem: private credit is among the fastest-growing asset classes, yet asset-backed lending in Latin America still runs on spreadsheets, e-mail, notaries (a podcast cites US$500 stamp fees in Mexico) and manual document checks. Fintechs find it hard to borrow debt, lenders cannot see their collateral, and every facility needs bespoke reporting. Logic and why now: as fintechs and non-bank lenders move from equity to debt funding, and global lenders such as Goldman Sachs enter the region, each facility needs a neutral layer that verifies assets, reconciles cash and gives the lender daily visibility. A software layer that sits between borrower and lender is paid per facility or per asset, and gets stickier once it is embedded in the legal process (verification agent, waivers, digital signature). Market: no published market size was read. Bottom-up, with assumptions: if US$20-60 billion of asset-backed and private credit facilities are outstanding in Latin America (assumption) and a platform earns 0.1-0.3% a year on the balances it verifies and services, the revenue pool is about US$20-180 million a year, with more if Mexico and other markets grow. What is different: it was built by a founder who worked on both sides of the facility and was adopted early by a global lender as verification agent, which gives it distribution that purely local competitors lack; Kanastra (Brazil, also in Norte's portfolio) is the closest regional comparable and appeared in the same searches, but the two were not compared. Fit with Norte (our reading, from the Manifesto read 2026-11-24): a young founder with unusually strong technical depth in the product she sells, which is the kind of founder profile the Manifesto describes. The sources do not place Norte in the seed (the company's own post lists every investor) or in any later round found, so how and when Norte took part is unknown. Risks: a small market in the near term, concentration in a few fintech borrowers and lenders, long enterprise sales and legal cycles, the entry of larger servicers and Brazilian players, and a business model whose pricing and revenue are not public.

value: US startup whose AI career agent, Lia, matches tech candidates with jobs and makes warm introductions to hiring managers; candidates pay 20% of their first month's salary only if hired and employers use it free.

Refer is a US startup, a public benefit corporation based in Palo Alto, that gives each job seeker an AI career agent called Lia. The candidate tells Lia what they are good at, what they want next, their salary range, location, company size and visa status; Lia then searches a base of about 7,000 open jobs at about 2,000 employers and, only when the candidate and the hiring manager both show interest, sends a warm email introduction instead of an application into a queue. It is free for the candidate until they are hired, and then the candidate pays 20% of the first month's salary; companies use it for free and can pay a priority tier of 20% of first-year salary to be shown first. The founder's argument is that job boards earn when vacancies stay open and recruiters are paid by employers, whereas Refer's client is the candidate. It was started in 2024 by Andre Hamra, a Brazilian entrepreneur and Stanford alumnus, who put up flyers at Stanford offering to help people find jobs. The service began with Stanford software-engineering alumni and moved to all tech workers across the US, and its program was being extended to about 20 more universities in 2026. Traction: by July 2026 it had set up nearly 6,000 interviews at more than 2,000 companies, with more than half of users getting an interview within 24 hours of an introduction, according to the company. In July 2026 it disclosed a previously unannounced US$7.5 million seed round led by Canary, bringing total funding to about US$10 million (after an earlier US$2.5 million round); the money is meant to add candidates and employers. The candidate-pays model is unusual and draws a regulatory question, as the International Labour Organization's Convention 181 bars worker fees in the countries that ratified it (not the US).

value: Problem: job seekers, above all in tech, send many applications that go unanswered, and recruiters and job boards work for the employer or profit when vacancies remain open. Employers receive floods of low-fit applications. Logic and why now: a language-model agent can read a profile and a job base, filter for mutual fit and write a credible introduction at near-zero marginal cost, so a placement fee that was once paid for human recruiters can be charged to the candidate for a larger share of wins and still be small against a tech salary (20% of one month's pay is about 1.7% of annual pay). Market: no market size was read. Bottom-up with assumptions: if the platform places 20,000 people a year at an average first-month salary of US$10,000 (assumption), a 20% fee is US$2,000 each and revenue is US$40 million; 100,000 placements would be US$200 million. US tech and professional hiring runs in the millions of hires a year (assumption, not sourced), so this is a small share of it. What is different: the candidate is the client, introductions are bilateral and warm, and employers pay nothing, so supply of jobs grows faster than in a model that charges them; established AI-recruiting vendors named in the press (Paradox, HireVue, Eightfold AI, Findem) sell to employers. Fit with Norte (our reading, from the Manifesto read 2026-11-24): a Brazilian founder building in Silicon Valley with a distribution trick (campus alumni networks), the sort of founder-led, network-driven start that Norte describes; the single source that lists Norte (a Spanish blog) calls it a follow-on investor, which would fit Norte's follower role after earlier support. Risks: the legality and acceptance of charging candidates (ILO and industry codes oppose it, and US states may regulate), collection risk once a candidate has the job, a crowded market of AI recruiting tools and large job platforms, and the dependence on a small team and one lead investor's round.

value: Malga is a Brazilian payments infrastructure company that lets digital businesses connect to many acquirers, anti-fraud tools, wallets and banks through one API, route each payment to the best option, and increasingly build their own payment products on top.

value: Malga (called Plug until early 2023) sells payments infrastructure to Brazilian digital businesses. A company that sells online normally has to integrate with each payment provider separately, a job that takes developers months, and it loses sales whenever its one provider declines a card or goes down. Malga gives it one API in front of more than 30 connections (acquirers, anti-fraud tools, digital wallets, banks and reconciliation providers, per its site; 20-plus processors in 2025 press). The customer builds a payment flow and chooses which provider handles each method; if the first provider declines, the payment is retried on the second and the third. Malga says its customers cut Pix costs by up to 90%, boleto costs by 50% and credit-card costs by up to 40%, and reduced declined transactions by 20%, recovering about R$170 million in lost sales by the end of 2024. The product has three layers, all on its site: orchestration (routing, split, recurrence, tokenization, anti-fraud); a white-label infrastructure (dashboard, payment links, checkout and SDKs under the client's own brand); and a payment processor, a sub-acquiring service of its own, so a platform can earn revenue on each transaction it processes, with settlement, split, reconciliation and receivables advance included. Its customers have included Petlove, Privalia, JCA and Ingresse; since about 2025 it has aimed mainly at B2B platforms (SaaS companies, ERPs, fintechs and digital banks) that want to turn payments into a product and a source of revenue. Malga earns from the volume it processes and from platform fees (the sources do not give the pricing). It was started in 2020, as Plug, by Alex Vilhena (CEO, formerly at Chute and PayPal's Braintree), Thiago Garuti (COO, formerly at Medicinae Solutions) and Marcel Nicolay (CTO, formerly at Zoop and Gympass), after Vilhena saw companies integrating many providers just to have a fallback. Plug went through Y Combinator in 2021 (which took about 7%), was then based in Rio de Janeiro, and raised a US$2.7 million seed in November 2021 led by Costanoa with QED, Verve Capital, Latitud and Norte Ventures; Costanoa led an extension in 2022. In February 2023 it rebranded as Malga (from amalgam), with 36 clients and a first client in Chile. Traction: revenue grew five times in 2022 according to the company, and Brazil Journal reports it five-folded in 2023 and tripled in 2024, when volume reached R$4 billion (R$5 billion annualized). In December 2024 it made its first acquisition, Drip, a Pix-instalment (buy now, pay later) start-up with about 30,000 users, to start offering consumer and merchant credit. In February 2025 it raised a R$32 million Series A led by iDEXO (TOTVS's venture arm) and Costanoa, with Ignia and Gaingels joining and QED, Norte and Y Combinator following on; the CEO said it was close to breakeven. Malga expected about R$15 billion in volume in 2025, three times 2024, and plans to double volume and revenue in 2026, focusing on Brazil, the evolution of Pix and ways to earn more from volume.

Each integration costs months of developer time, any provider outage or card decline loses a sale, and Malga's CEO cites one in four e-commerce purchases denied in Brazil against under 5% in developed markets (Brazil Journal, 2025). Market (our estimate): Abecs reports R$4.5 trillion in card payments in 2025 (R$3.1 trillion credit). Pix, boleto and other methods add to the volume Malga orchestrates, but no read source gives total online payment volume, so we do not size the whole. Malga processed about R$5 billion in 2024 and projected R$15 billion for 2025, about 0.3% of card volume alone. Latin America beyond Brazil is upside, not in the estimate. What is different: Malga is both an orchestrator and a processor with a white-label stack, so platforms can launch a payments product without becoming acquirers, and it owns a small credit line from Drip. Payment orchestrators elsewhere (Yuno, another Norte portfolio company, and Spreedly abroad; our naming, not read) suggest the model is real, and the CEO names merchants' inertia, not a competitor, as the main rival. Fit with Norte: Norte followed on in the seed and the Series A, which fits its connector role at a stage where founders need funds and a network (our reading of the Manifesto, not Norte's statement); the founders have payments experience (Braintree, Zoop, Gympass). Risks: the take rate falls as volume grows and large customers negotiate; value depends on a few big acquirers and wallets; the credit business adds risk; and the target market has moved more than once (Plug, Malga, B2B platforms).

value: Cayena is a business-to-business marketplace where restaurants, bars, bakeries, hotels, dark kitchens, schools, caterers and small markets buy their groceries and supplies from many suppliers in one place. Before platforms like it, an owner either spent hours in wholesale stores comparing prices and queuing, or negotiated one by one with distributors over WhatsApp, with no guarantee of the best price (Norte's case post found a 60% price gap for the same bag of rice across 15 suppliers on one day). Cayena pre-qualifies the suppliers (the company said in 2021 that only about 30% of candidates are accepted), shows a real-time catalogue (more than 100 suppliers and 50,000 items by 2024), recommends the best mix of suppliers for each basket on price and convenience, and offers next-day delivery, free freight and a dedicated account consultant. It makes money mainly as a commission paid by the suppliers on the demand it brings them, and, through Cayena Pay, from a credit layer: launched in early 2022 as buy-now-pay-later, it lets the restaurant pay the supplier on term while the supplier is paid promptly, so the financing arm both helps the buyer's working capital and keeps default away from the suppliers. By 2024 the company said more than R$2 billion in credit had been made available in three years, with an approval rate 50% above the industry average, backed by relationships with Itaú, Safra, Santander and Allianz. Cayena is asset-light: it handles neither inventory nor logistics, which separates it from Colombia's Frubana and Brazil's Pantore, which buy and deliver the goods (Brazil Journal, 2022). The three founders met at Insper in 2011: Gabriel Sendacz (private equity at NEO Investimentos), Pedro Carvalho (investment banking at Merrill Lynch) and Raymond Shayo (investment banking at JP Morgan). In 2018 they left finance to start a company and chose the sector with a checklist (a B2B, recurring, offline, large and fragmented market, with a win-win model) after looking at cemeteries and healthcare; Carvalho's family runs a Japanese food delivery kitchen in Salvador, which tested the first tool, with a reported 20% drop in the cost of goods sold. The MVP went live in September 2019 in São Paulo. Problem: Brazil has about 1.1 million food service outlets that spend over US$35 billion a year on supplies (Norte case post), most of them small and family-run. They buy by phone, WhatsApp, or by visiting wholesalers, with no price transparency (a 60% spread on one bag of rice across 15 suppliers) and stock-outs of up to 10%; suppliers, for their part, fear unpaid invoices. Logic: a marketplace that pre-qualifies suppliers, optimises the basket and guarantees payment to suppliers (through Cayena Pay) removes the buyer's search cost and the supplier's credit risk, and takes a commission on recurring purchases (clients bought five to seven times a month in 2021 to 2022). Asset-light operation lets growth use little cash. Market: the Norte post puts Brazil's food service procurement at over US$35 billion a year, and Cayena's CEO and Norte put Latin America at about US$200 billion (company and investor figure; not an independent source). Cayena moved about R$1 billion a year in 2024, roughly 0.5% of Brazil's US$35 billion (R$190 billion at about R$5.4 per US dollar, our conversion), so even a 5% share would mean US$1.75 billion of purchases a year; at a 3% to 5% commission-plus-credit revenue (our assumption, not sourced) that is about US$50 to US$90 million of revenue, a rough order of magnitude for Brazil alone. What is different: it is asset-light (no inventory or trucks) while Frubana and Pantore buy and deliver (Brazil Journal, 2022), which keeps capital needs low; it owns the credit and payment layer, which is the real trust problem between small buyers and suppliers; and its team is from finance, which suits that layer. Fit with Norte: Norte backed it at the seed (2020), followed on in the Series A and the Series B, and wrote a case post on it, consistent with its pattern of following strong founders with a network of funds (our reading of the Manifesto). Risks: credit losses in a sector with thin margins; bigger rivals with logistics scale, such as Frubana or distributors with their own apps; and the 2024 plan to expand to 500 cities needs a heavy sales force. Evidence is thin on profits (breakeven not confirmed).

value: Quansa lets employers pay frontline workers the moment they earn the money, instead of at the end of the month, and ties that pay to attendance and performance. An employer connects Quansa to its time-clock and payroll systems; when an employee finishes a shift, sells, receives a tip or reaches a target, the amount becomes available in an app straight away, and the employer still pays once a month (the company fronts the advance and the employer settles with Quansa at month end). Quansa says this is not a loan, and the employee's own earned wages are what is advanced. Its pitch is operational: less absenteeism, less turnover, a more stable operation, with no extra work for HR or finance and no change to payroll. Customers have reported up to 50% fewer absences and up to 30% lower turnover (company claims). The Brazilian site lists several products: on-demand pay, instant tips, instant commissions, incentive campaigns, and management and payment of intermittent workers and freelancers (Quansa Extras). Its customers include a McDonald's franchisee with more than 500 employees, Grupo Fit (more than 10 brands, airport operations), Grupo Alife Nino and, in Chile, LimChile, Derco and Ultramar. It shows ISO 27001, LGPD and SOC 1 compliance, and its product was designed with labor-law lawyers. At the start the company sold financial health as an employee benefit, like a Gympass for finances, with financial coaching and salary advances, and said it earned only a per-employee fee from the employer, never interest or lending margin (Startups.com.br, 2021); by 2026 its Brazilian pitch had moved to frontline retention, in a context where, it says, the updated NR-1 workplace rule makes financial stress an employer responsibility. It was founded in the second half of 2020 in Chile by Gonzalo Blanco (Uruguayan, CEO, ex-McKinsey and Stanford GSB, who had always been the family's financial adviser) and Mafalda Barros (Portuguese, COO, also ex-McKinsey and Stanford GSB, in Latin America since 2013). Pear VC, the first investor, backed them at Stanford. Quansa launched in Chile in late 2020 and began operating in Brazil in June 2021; in July 2021 it announced a US$3.6 million seed led by Valor Capital Group with Pear VC, Canary, Norte, Magma, Sequoia Scouts and angels (Ariel Lambrecht of 99, Gupy's Mariana Dias and Bruna Guimarães, Volanty's Maurício Feldman, Branch's Mada Seghete). The team then had 10 people; the money was for technology and doubling the team. Brazil is now its main market, with a Brazilian company opened in March 2021 and based in São Paulo, and Chile remains a market; no later round was found.

value: Problem: frontline workers in retail and food service live on monthly paychecks, so a bill that cannot wait pushes them toward payday loans or toward skipping a shift to do gig work, which employers see as absenteeism and turnover. Brazil had 57.1 million formal jobs at the end of 2024 (RAIS), and the Quansa site says 82% of retailers report rising turnover. Logic: if pay arrives the same day, workers keep their main job; the employer pays Quansa once a month and gains attendance and retention, so the employer is the buyer and the bill is a fee per employee, not interest on loans. Why now: platform work (delivery, ride-hailing) set an expectation of instant pay; Pix makes small instant transfers cheap; and the employer-side pain of turnover is rising. Market (our estimate): of RAIS's 57.1 million formal jobs, we assume 8 to 12 million are frontline positions in retail, foodservice, facilities and logistics that fit the model (our assumption; the RAIS summary lists commerce at about 10 million in a page we did not read). If an employer pays Quansa R$10 to R$20 per employee per month (our assumption; pricing is not public), full penetration would be R$1 billion to R$3 billion a year, and 3% to 5% of that, a realistic target for a Brazilian leader, is R$30 to R$150 million of revenue: a rough order of magnitude. Chile and other markets add a smaller upside. What is different: Quansa links pay to attendance and incentive rules (so it is a retention tool, not just a wage advance), integrates with time clocks and payroll, advances the money itself and bills the employer, and says it does not earn from credit interest. Competition in on-demand pay is dense (benefit apps, payroll fintechs and banks; our knowledge, not read), so the differentiation is retention results and integration. Fit with Norte: it is a follower in the seed, next to Valor, Canary and Pear, which matches its pattern of joining at the seed with strong funds (our reading of the Manifesto); founders are McKinsey and Stanford operators with a clear problem, though the story moved from a financial-health benefit to frontline retention. Risks: rising cost of capital for advancing wages; regulation of wage advance; customer concentration in a few chains; and no financing round found since 2021, so growth may have been funded from revenue (unknown).

value: Sanii organises home care for older people in Brazil. Families that need a caregiver, nursing technician or physiotherapist for a parent or grandparent come to Sanii, which selects, trains and places professionals with them, assures the payment and the replacement of the professional, and keeps monitoring the older person's condition with a team of gerontologists and nurses, available 24 hours a day by its own account. The founders call it a closed marketplace: thousands apply each month and only about 3% are approved, after screening, experience checks, background checks and interviews, and nearly 30 factors (distance, skills, availability) are crossed to match a caregiver with a family. Most permanent-shift clients stay one to two years, usually until the patient dies, and Sanii reallocates the caregiver to another family, which gives caregivers more stable work in a sector that is otherwise informal and fragmented. Revenue comes from what the families pay for care, with the professionals' pay deducted (the sources do not give prices or margins). Technology is used behind the care: a system called Care IA, built on Google's Gemini, refines the match between caregivers and patients; AI agents interview candidates and collect new clients' needs; and an AI assistant on WhatsApp helps caregivers during the shift, writing handover reports and reminding them of medication times. Sanii also trains caregivers (for example in palliative care and handling devices), and sells courses. The long-term plan, according to InfoMoney, adds medicine and vaccine delivery, dental care and smart sensors and cameras. Its history has two parts. The company was started by Renato Tilkian (a health executive with more than 20 years' experience, who led Amil's roll-up and consolidated Lavebras and Vitus), Michael Kapps (Canadian founder of mental-health start-up Vitalk, bought by Gympass/Wellhub in 2022) and Angelina Clarke (ex-McKinsey, founder of the recruiting start-up AssuredLabor, former head of strategy at Descomplica). In October 2023 it announced a R$8 million pre-seed led by Valor Capital Group, with 15 other investors including GreenRock and Norte Ventures, then a prevention service: weekly home visits of up to 90 minutes to stimulate memory, body and social life of people over 60, in 28 São Paulo neighbourhoods, with a physical space planned in Higienópolis, a team of 12, and a target of 30 clients by the end of the year. The founders later bought Senior Services, a traditional home-care company founded by gerontologist Margherita Mizan (about 14 years old), and merged it into Sanii, which is why the site says it has more than 14 years in elder care. Traction: the company says its monthly recurring revenue grew six-fold in 18 months, that it had delivered half a million hours of care by December 2025, and that it expected to grow 300% in 2025. In late 2025 it closed a R$5 million follow-on round led by Sororitê Ventures (total raised R$13 million), used for expansion to the interior and coast of São Paulo and for technology. In mid-2026 it opened an office in Campinas and said it will enter eight more cities, by organic growth and acquisitions (the ABC region, Alphaville, Brasília, Recife, Salvador, Goiânia and Porto Alegre are mapped), aiming to be the largest home-care company in Latin America.
