value: Problem: Brazil is ageing fast; in 2023 IBGE counted for the first time more older people than young, and the share aged 60 or over rose from 8.7% in 2000 to 15.6% in 2023 (InfoMoney). Families that want an older relative to stay at home (aging in place) have to find caregivers in an informal, fragmented market, with no guarantee of quality or replacement, while caregivers face irregular income and unpaid work. A study of Unifesp reports 1.76 million Brazilians over 60 with dementia, a number expected to triple by 2050 (Startupi, quoting Unifesp and the Ministry of Health). Logic: a company that selects strictly (about 3% accepted), trains, guarantees payment and replacement, and matches with data can charge a premium and keep caregivers loyal; AI in the back office (matching, recruiting, handover reports) lowers cost per hour and error. Why now: demographic change, a family structure with fewer relatives available, and cheap AI for operations. Market (our estimate): 15.6% of Brazil's population of about 203 million (IBGE 2022 Census, our recollection; not read) is about 32 million people aged 60 or over. If 2% to 3% of them (0.6 to 1 million, our assumption) pay for home care at R$3,000 to R$6,000 a month (our assumption), spending is roughly R$20 billion to R$70 billion a year; it is a rough order of magnitude for professional home care in Brazil. If Sanii reached 1% to 2% of that spending, revenue would be R$200 million to R$1.4 billion. Latin America is upside. What is different: it operates the care (clinical team, replacement guarantee), not a classified-ads marketplace; the founders pair a health-sector operator (Tilkian), a startup operator who sold a company to Gympass (Kapps) and a McKinsey-trained operator (Clarke); and it owns a heritage brand (Senior Services). Fit with Norte: Norte joined the pre-seed with Valor, an early-round pattern that suits connecting a new team to funds and talent (our reading of the Manifesto, not Norte's statement). Risks: it is a service business with labour-intensive margins and caregiver supply as the bottleneck; unit economics are not public; roll-ups outside São Paulo are hard to integrate; competition from established home-care firms and health plans; and the change of strategy from prevention to caregivers within two years.

value: Vendah is a Brazilian reselling marketplace for people who sell products to their own contacts and over social media, usually women looking for extra or main income. A reseller signs up for free (adult with a bank account in her own name), picks products on the Vendah app, shares photos with her network, and orders what she sold; Vendah ships to her, with free freight on larger orders, and she keeps the margin between her price and the price of the kit. The product line has changed. When it raised its seed in 2023, Vendah sold more than 700 low-ticket items for home, kitchen, decor and babies, bought from importers and distributors and stored in its own distribution centre; the reseller needed no minimum purchase or demo kit and earned a 15% to 20% commission paid within two business days. Today its site is organised around beauty: it sells the internet's favourite beauty brands to resellers, with instalments at no interest and without a credit card, and with support from specialists on WhatsApp. The Y Combinator profile describes this as a marketplace connecting digital-first beauty brands to a network of individual sellers, powered by embedded microcredit and a proprietary credit engine, and says that after the pivot to marketplace plus credit, GMV was growing about 30% a month, with close to 1,000 active sellers and positive, improving risk-adjusted margins. The company makes money on the margin of the goods it sells to resellers and, in the credit model, on the financing that lets a reseller pay in instalments without a card (the sources do not give the numbers). It is a cousin of the traditional direct-selling industry: the ABEVD reported R$45 billion in direct sales in Brazil in 2022 (Startups.com.br), and Startupi counts more than 5 million women in the channel. It was started in 2021 by Luis Felipe Franco (CEO; created Endeavor Brazil's Scale-up Endeavor programme and led growth at the beauty brand Sallve), Marcelo Canovas (an administrator since the company's registration in May 2021; the COO's Y Combinator biography says he co-founded Liv Up and a software house) and, according to a single directory, Pedro Pedruzzi as CTO. Before it had operations it raised an R$8.5 million pre-seed in 2021 led by Maya Capital, with Norte Ventures, Village Global and angels from 99, Creditas, MadeiraMadeira and Sallve. It went through Y Combinator in the Winter 2023 batch and in August 2023 announced an R$12 million (about US$2.4 million) seed, with YC, Goodwater and Domo Invest and angels in the US, India and China; the CEO said the money gave it the option to reach breakeven before a Series A and that it expected to grow five times in 2023 and to expand from São Paulo and the coast to Rio de Janeiro and Belo Horizonte in 2024. At that time it had served more than 30,000 informal resellers. No later round was found.

value: Jitter is a web-based motion design tool, pitched as Figma for motion: a designer who can lay out a screen, a brand asset or a social post should be able to animate it without learning a timeline-heavy program such as After Effects. Users import designs (most often from Figma through its plugin, and since October 2025 from Figma Buzz, plus images and vector shapes), animate layers with presets, curved paths, morphing shapes, gradients and blur on an infinite canvas, collaborate with product and marketing teammates in a shared workspace, and export to video (up to 4K, .mov, .mp4, .webm), GIF and Lottie for apps and websites. Its site says more than 20,000 creative teams use it, with customer stories from Perplexity, Deliveroo and the design studio 27b. The recent product focus is AI and production at scale. Users can describe an effect in words and get an editable animation; Jitter AI generates variations, turns still images into video, and, since July 2026, 'Superagents' built into the editor can remix templates, animate complex scenes from scratch and turn one asset into a campaign of many sizes, formats and languages, with batch export. A Brand Kit (beta, November 2026) stores a brand's colours, text styles and easings, and the product can be driven by an AI assistant through an MCP connection. It sells subscriptions per editor per month (a free plan with 3 files, 720p export and a limited AI allowance; paid plans called Max and Ultra, whose prices were not readable). Directory sites list Norte Ventures among its early backers, but no readable source describes the round, so the amounts and Norte's participation remain unverified. value: Caveo is a financial and accounting platform for doctors who work as legal entities (PJ). Since 2015, when hospitals were allowed to hire physicians as PJ, a large share of doctors have had to open a company, issue invoices for each hospital shift, pay taxes and keep books, a bureaucratic job that newly graduated doctors, living off on-call shifts, handle badly. Caveo handles it in an app and on WhatsApp: it opens the company, issues invoices, debits taxes automatically, keeps the accounts, receives payments by Pix in a PJ account and suggests how much to transfer to the doctor's personal account. It added tools specific to doctors, such as a shift calendar, a wallet with useful information and a tax simulator, plus an AI assistant on WhatsApp, and it runs community activities (networking between new graduates and experienced doctors, learning tracks and help to win the first shifts). Revenue came almost entirely from subscriptions: R$147, R$247 or R$397 a month depending on the doctor's billing (average ticket about R$250 a month in 2025). The company is moving customers from the software service to its own bank account and plans to add investments, credit cards, insurance and pension products; a first financial product, 'guaranteed receipt' (an advance on the 30 to 90 days that hospitals take to pay doctors), was planned for the second quarter of 2026. Its go-to-market goes through medical schools: it says it operates in 93% of Brazil's medical schools, reached an estimated 8% of the 2023 graduates, 18% in 2024 and about 40% in 2025, and gets 95% of its sales by referral with an NPS close to 90 (company figures). After building 'almost a new company' in the second half of 2025 to serve experienced doctors with more complex taxes (Lucro Presumido instead of Simples, office doctors and surgeons), those now make up 30% of new customers. The company was founded in São Paulo by Wilgo Cavalcante (CEO), who saw the demand while doing accounting consulting for a client and moved to São Paulo and to the Link School of Business, where he met co-founder Lorenço Boettcher; the sources date the start to 2021 (registry, Baguete) or 2022 (Brazil Journal, NeoFeed). It raised R$6.5 million from a pool of doctors, then in June 2024 a round of about US$1 million with R$2 million from Afya's venture arm and angels such as iFood co-founder Guilherme Bonifácio and Alan Chusid of Spin Pay, which gave it access to Afya's 32 medical schools and its White Book app used by about 45% of Brazilian doctors. In February 2025 it raised R$20 million led by Kortex Ventures (whose investors include Fleury, Sabin and Bradesco Seguros) with ONEVC, Zenda and Norte Ventures, and in December 2025 closed the Series A at R$54 million in total with a R$34 million tranche led by Zenda that brought in Enseada, the family office of SulAmérica's founders. Traction: about 10,000 doctors in February 2025 and more than 20,000 by December, growth of 400% in 2024, annualised recurring revenue of about R$25 million in November 2025 and a projection of R$50 million in January 2026. Its closest comparable in the sector is Contabilizei, the market leader in online accounting with a PJ account.

value: Level (levelai.com.br; the company was called NeuralMed until April 2026) sells an intelligence layer for hospitals, health insurers, clinics and diagnostic networks. It reads clinical data from the systems they already run (electronic records such as Tasy and MV, imaging systems RIS and PACS, reports and prescriptions), joins it with operational and financial data, and turns it into actions with a measurable financial return. The site gives examples: AI that reads radiology reports and finds critical findings that were never acted on (for instance a nodule noticed in an exam done for another reason), a risk score by disease, exams, drugs and history, the 2% of patients who concentrate 80% of costs found before admission, more than 120 clinical triggers that start traceable actions, and a path from exam to finding to protocol to procedure to revenue that can be audited. A WhatsApp assistant contacts patients to schedule visits or warn them of a needed test, and the platform covers oncology, asthma, diabetes and hypertension. Customers include hospitals Moinhos de Vento and Mãe de Deus and Santa Casa, in Porto Alegre. The business model changed in 2025. Software had been sold as separate algorithms with six-month to one-year deployments; the offer is now two software-as-a-service packages (Light and Full), implemented in 4 to 8 weeks with about 90% of the work done by Level's team, and the company promises it will not charge if agreed targets are not met in the agreed time, which cut the sales cycle from more than 180 days to 30 to 60 days. A new customer type is the pharmaceutical industry, which benefits from early diagnosis of cancer; the first contracts were with Adium (Uruguay) and an unnamed European company. It was started in 2018 as NeuralMed by Anthony Eigier (CEO; founder of the startup accelerator Tree Labs and co-founder of the mobile-games company Fanatee) and radiologist André Castilla (CMO), to apply artificial intelligence to medical images and texts. Its first products were TrIA, for triage in hospitals and laboratories, and Atlas, launched in 2022, for monitoring chronic and oncology patients and for pharma. It raised R$3.2 million in March 2021 from Alexia Ventures, Norte Ventures, MG Tech and the IDB, then R$10 million in August 2021 led by the health insurer Grupo NotreDame Intermédica (which took 9.29%), and in 2022 a round led by Good Karma Ventures, its third in 18 months, with 5 million lives in its customers' bases; NeoFeed counts US$7.7 million raised in total from NotreDame Intermédica, the IDB, Kortex Ventures and GK Ventures. By June 2025 the company had reached its lowest point, with monthly recurring revenue under R$100,000 and only eight clients. After a nine-month reset with Mariana Gaspers (a former finance and revenue executive at Twilio, Hilab and Ascential, who joined in September 2024 and became founding partner), it relaunched in April 2026 as Level, with 36 clients, annual recurring revenue up from under R$1.2 million to R$5 million, and a further R$10 million contracted, with the aim of growing it by the end of 2026 (company figures to NeoFeed). Its algorithms, it says, run 350 times faster than a human reviewer and are close to 500 times.

Problem: Brazilian hospitals, insurers and labs hold large amounts of clinical data (reports, exams, records) that nobody reads at scale, so critical findings are missed, high-cost patients are identified late and revenue and prevention opportunities go unseen, while insurers' medical costs keep rising (operators' operating profit fell 10% to R$5.6 billion in the first half of 2026, Folha de Pernambuco). Logic: an AI layer that connects to existing systems (Tasy, MV, RIS, PACS), finds the few patients who drive cost or revenue and triggers an action can be paid for by the financial result it shows; the offer 'no result, no fee' lowers the buyer's risk. Why now: language models and vision models make reading reports and records cheap, and payers need to cut medical-loss ratios. Market (our estimate): Brazil has 53.1 million private health-plan beneficiaries and 698 medical operators (ANS, via O Liberal, September 2026), plus thousands of hospitals, clinics and labs. If 300 institutions (operators, hospitals and diagnostic networks, our assumption) paid R$0.5 million to R$2 million a year (our assumption; Level's ARR is R$5 million for 36 clients, about R$140,000 each, so the assumption is a reach for much larger deals), the market would be R$150 million to R$600 million a year in Brazil; pharma contracts for early diagnosis and Latin America add upside. Level's present R$5 million ARR is therefore a small share, and the case rests on enlarging the average contract. What is different: it sells results, not algorithms, integrates without replacing systems, and combines clinical and financial data; its radiologist co-founder and a customer base of Porto Alegre hospitals give clinical credibility. value: Jusfy is a Brazilian legal-tech platform that sells lawyers a single subscription with dozens of tools, and describes itself as the operating system of the Brazilian lawyer. It started with calculators for the everyday numbers of legal practice (alimony, bank-financing and abusive-interest reviews, FGTS, rent debts, labour and civil calculations), then added searches by CPF, CNPJ or licence plate to find a debtor's assets, a jurisprudence search across Brazilian courts, a bank of petition templates, electronic signature and, from 2025, JusProcessos (case workflow management, sold as an add-on) and JusGPT, an AI assistant that drafts petitions, summarises cases, reviews documents and transcribes WhatsApp audio. The company also sells website building and marketing tools for lawyers, a lawyer-client matching feature and, in 2026, Jusfy Pay, a payments and billing product that is the first step of a financial-services line for lawyers. The business is a subscription: in 2022 plans cost R$59 to R$97 a month depending on the number of searches, and today there are three plans (One, Ultimate, Black) with a 7-day free trial, plus customised packages for law firms, legal departments and municipalities, and partnerships with state bars (OABs). The company was founded by Rafael Saccol Bagolin, a lawyer from Rio Grande do Sul who had practised since 2010, with software engineer Juliano Lima and lawyer Cristian Bastianello; the registry shows the company opening on 26 January 2021. Bagolin has said the company was bootstrapped, had cash and was already at breakeven before its outside rounds. Traction: about 4,500 subscribers and R$300 thousand of monthly revenue in November 2022; 14 thousand clients at the start of 2024 and 28 thousand at its end, with R$25 million of revenue in 2024; 30 thousand clients in March 2025, 47 thousand and a team of 72 in August 2025; more than R$50 million of annual revenue in 2025 (up about 118%) and more than 60 thousand active professionals in 2026, with the state bars of Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro and others among its clients. Backers: a R$7 million seed in December 2022 led by SaaSholic with Norte Ventures; a pre-Series A in March 2025 at about US$30 million valuation with MAYA Capital, SaaSholic, Norte, FJ Labs and The Legal Tech Fund; and a US$15 million Series A in July 2026 led by Quona Capital, the first Brazilian investment of Thomson Reuters Ventures. The money goes to financial services for lawyers (Jusfy Pay, credit), new AI products and a version for law students.

value: Problem: Brazil has about 1.5 million registered lawyers (OAB register, November 2026, via Advbox), 72% of them self-employed (OAB and FGV's Perfil ADV study), and the CEO says about 87% work alone or in small firms. These professionals spend hours on low-value work, such as calculating alimony, reviewing financing contracts, searching for debtors' assets, drafting standard petitions and chasing clients for fees, with a patchwork of tools and no finance department; banks also treat lawyers as difficult customers (irregular income, they sue banks). The courts received 40.9 million new cases in 2025 (a record), so the workload keeps growing. Logic and why now: a cheap, all-in-one subscription removes the need to buy many point tools, calculators are a proven entry point because they save money immediately, and generative AI lets the same subscriber draft and review work that used to need a junior associate (Bagolin's stated view is that AI makes the solo lawyer 'superpowered'). The data and daily use of the platform give the company what banks lack to price credit to lawyers, which is the fintech step (Jusfy Pay, receivables advance). Market and reachable share: our own bottom-up estimate, not a sourced market size. Brazil has 1.5 million lawyers, of whom roughly 1.1 million are autonomous. Jusfy's 60 thousand active professionals are about 4% of all lawyers. If a strong outcome reaches 10% to 25% of lawyers (150 to 375 thousand) at R$1,000 to R$2,000 a year (its 2025 revenue of more than R$50 million over about 50 thousand clients is roughly R$1,000 per client, an assumption), the subscription market is about R$150 million to R$750 million a year in Brazil alone, and payments and credit could add revenue per user (Quona cites Toast and Shopify as the pattern). What is different: Jusfy started from calculators and searches and now bundles AI, workflow, payments and credit for the solo and small-firm lawyer, a segment large vendors tend to ignore; it grew from R$300 thousand a month in late 2022 to above R$4 million a month in 2025 while reportedly at breakeven. The sources read do not name competitors; Clio is the best-known comparable abroad (legal software plus payments), but no page with its figures could be read, so no figure is used. Fit with Norte: our reading is that a founder who is a practising lawyer, paired with an engineer, a bootstrapped business with revenue from early on, and a need for strong funds and operators on the cap table (SaaSholic, MAYA, FJ Labs, Quona, Thomson Reuters) fit Norte's stated model of backing obsessed founders and bringing top funds and talent; Norte was in the seed and the pre-Series A. Risks: regulation of the legal profession (a Startups.com.br headline says OAB-RJ allows AI but restricts legal-tech intermediation models), generative AI that large vendors or model providers can bundle, and a credit business that needs capital and risk control; the fintech launch slipped from September 2025 to 2026.
note: Market size is our bottom-up estimate: lawyers 1,515,039 (OAB register, Advbox page read, dated 2026-11-18); 72% autonomous (Perfil ADV, same page); 60k active (Baguete 2026) is 4% of 1.5M; R$50M revenue / about 50k clients (Startups.com.br 2026-03-06) is about R$1,000 per client; 10-25% x 1.5M x R$1,000-2,000 = R$150M-R$750M (assumptions). Courts: 40.9M new cases in 2025 (Advbox). The OAB-RJ resolution comes from a Startups.com.br headline only (article not read), a lead. value: Elevva is an Argentine company that buys and partners with e-commerce brands in Latin America and helps small and mid-sized sellers scale them. It was started in 2021 by three Argentine e-commerce operators, Félix Elizalde, Maximiliano Chab and Aníbal de Frankenberg, who had run brands sold on the region's marketplaces, in categories such as home and garden, apparel, computing and electronics. The original idea was the 'e-commerce aggregator': Elevva would acquire or partner with leading sellers and put in its team, its technology and its capital, while the sellers brought their product knowledge, building a portfolio of brands that share logistics, sourcing and software across countries. From day one it also developed its own brands in categories where it saw no partners and set up its own operation in China. Its site today describes a wider menu for pymes: selling a brand to Elevva's portfolio; regionalisation (entering new countries with its infrastructure, logistics and regulatory know-how); a SaaS to run multichannel sales, inventory and shipping from one place together with a logistics operator; working-capital financing, which it launched as a lending unit in 2022; and product development and sourcing in China for private labels. The company says it moved from only acquiring brands to being a strategic partner for small businesses. The sources read do not say how it earns from each line, nor give revenue, headcount or the brands it owns. Timeline: it announced its Colombian launch in December 2021, seeking about 50 partner companies there; in December 2021 it made an offer for the Chilean fitness-equipment brand BodyTrainer, a deal that closed in April 2022; and in May 2022 it announced a US$30 million seed round with Asymmetric Capital, MatterScale Ventures, Canary, Redwood Ventures, Latitud, BluStone, Primo Ventures, Norte, Stanford GSB's 23Fund, Bolt Ventures and angels such as Pierpaolo Barbieri (Ualá), Ariel Lambrecht (99) and Matt Robinson (GoCardless), to keep adding brands, invest in technology and start the lending unit. The BodyTrainer purchase later became a dispute: the sellers say Elevva paid only the first half of the price (about UF 197,881, roughly 6 billion Chilean pesos) and sold inventory below cost, and in late 2025 they filed a criminal complaint for fraud in Chile after a Santiago arbitration court ordered Elevva to pay the balance with interest; Elevva denies any fraud, says the sellers hid information and has appealed the arbitral award. The matter is unresolved in the sources read. It matters for anyone assessing the company's acquisition model.

value: Problem: in Latin America small and mid-sized businesses that sell online lack three things at once: regional scale (each country has its own marketplaces, logistics and rules), working capital, and operating know-how in logistics, inventory and marketing. Many founders also have no exit for a good brand. The founders' own reading in 2022 was that the opportunity in Latin America is large and different from other regions because e-commerce penetration is low and small firms have little access to capital. Logic and why now: a consolidator that buys or partners with brands, then shares software, logistics and sourcing from China across countries, can raise margins and growth on brands that are too small for big retailers; adding a lending unit and a SaaS turns the same expertise into services to non-acquired sellers. The 2020-2021 e-commerce boom gave sellers brands worth buying and gave investors an appetite for 'aggregators'. Market and share: no independent regional market size was read. As a size indicator, Argentina's e-commerce chamber (CACE) reported that Argentine online retail sold 645 million units in 2025, with sales of about 35.3 trillion pesos, up 60% nominally against 31% inflation (preliminary results, Revista Mercado); converting that figure to dollars needs an exchange rate we did not read, so we give no US figure. A strong outcome would be a portfolio and services platform across Argentina, Chile, Colombia and Mexico, but the sources do not disclose Elevva's revenue, so we cannot estimate its share. What is different: it combines acquisition with services and, according to its founders, with an operation in China and its own software; most Latin American peers are marketplaces or software vendors. Comparables abroad are cautionary: Thrasio, the leading Amazon aggregator, filed for Chapter 11 in February 2024 with about US$495 million of debt cut, after the roll-up craze faded with slowing e-commerce growth (CNBC). Fit with Norte: our reading is that a seed of US$30 million with global and regional funds, led by three operators with direct e-commerce experience, matches Norte's stated interest in obsessed founders and in bringing top funds onto the cap table; Norte joined as one of many investors in the seed, a follower role. Risks: the aggregator model depends on paying fair prices and integrating brands, and the BodyTrainer dispute (arbitral award against Elevva, criminal complaint, reputation) is direct evidence of the main risk; thin transparency (no revenue, no brand list, no news of a later round); macro volatility in Argentina; and competition from Chinese platforms such as Temu and Shein in categories like apparel (Forbes Argentina headline, not read).

value: BotCity is a Brazilian software company, based in Campinas, that began as a code-first RPA (robotic process automation) tool and is now positioning itself as the governance and orchestration layer for Python automations and AI-generated scripts inside companies. It was started in 2020 by Lorhan Caproni (CEO, previously founder of the social-impact edtech Phomenta) and Gabriel Archanjo (CTO). Their bet went against the market: instead of drag-and-drop flowcharts for business users, as UiPath or Automation Anywhere sell, BotCity let developers write automations directly in Python, using computer vision to operate any screen, including desktop and legacy systems with no API, and added a platform to schedule, monitor and audit the robots. Early customers were technology-intensive Brazilian startups that used it, for example, to automate supplier approval (a task of up to ten days done by hand) or to integrate their products with customers' ERPs. Products today, on its English-language site, are an Orchestrator (scheduling, CI/CD, versioned and isolated runtimes, workload distribution, retries and logs for business-critical Python) and a tool, announced as Sentinel in 2025 and shown on the site as Sprav, that discovers code created by employees and their AI agents on endpoints, applies company policy and decides before execution what may run. The pitch is that once ChatGPT, Gemini or Copilot return Python for any request to 'automate this', every employee can create code that runs outside IT's control (shadow AI), with risks of leaked sensitive data, flawed code and dependence on one person. BotCity says its customers include Bayer, LG, XP, QuintoAndar, Stone, Raia Drogasil and Sicredi (Startups.com.br, 2025), and it runs a distributed, remote team. It does not disclose customer count or revenue. Funding: a R$15 million seed in December 2021 co-led by Astella and the SoftBank Latin America Fund with Alexia Ventures, Norte Ventures and angels; admission to Y Combinator's Winter 2022 batch; and a R$65 million Series A announced on 25 September 2025 led by Four Rivers, with Y Combinator, Astella and Upload. The money is to fund global expansion (offices in the US and UK are targeted) and research on new products such as Sentinel.

value: Problem: companies automate more and more of their operations with scripts, and since generative AI began returning working Python for any request (the CEO dates the turn to 2023-24), people outside IT create automations that run on company machines with no audit, access policy or owner. The IT Forum interview cites IBM's 2025 Cost of a Data Breach report, saying 87% of Brazilian companies still have no formal AI-governance policy, and surveys that 40% to 65% of employees at large companies use AI tools their IT area has not approved (figures as quoted by the article, we did not read the IBM report). Logic and why now: BotCity has been building the infrastructure to run, version, schedule and monitor Python automations since before the AI wave, so it is positioned to sell governance when the volume of scripts explodes. UiPath's CEO makes the same argument in 2026: when software gets cheaper to build, more gets built and the value shifts to the platforms that govern and orchestrate it (diginomica, March 2026; a vendor's view). Market and reachable share: no independent size for 'Python governance' exists, since the category is new. As rough anchors: the RPA market is projected at US$7.64 billion by 2028 (StartupHub, a secondary source quoting a forecast, treat as an order of magnitude), and UiPath, the listed leader, ended its fiscal year in January 2026 with US$1.853 billion of annual recurring revenue and US$1.611 billion of revenue (diginomica). A strong outcome for BotCity would be a niche but global enterprise-software business: for example 500 enterprise customers paying US$50 to US$150 thousand a year (our assumption) is US$25 to US$75 million of recurring revenue, about 1.5% to 4% of UiPath's ARR. What is different: it is built by developers for developers and started in code, while the large RPA vendors started from low-code for business users; it pairs governance with execution (Orchestrator) rather than only scanning for risks, it has a team already distributed and, per its CEO, a global structure from the start, and it is backed by Astella, SoftBank, Four Rivers and Y Combinator. Competitors named by the sources: UiPath and Automation Anywhere (RPA), plus the new AI governance vendors that the articles do not name. Fit with Norte: our reading is that two technical founders who built a global-first company out of Campinas, whose product needs distribution and top funds and operators on the cap table, match Norte's stated model of backing obsessed founders and bringing top funds to the cap table; Norte joined the seed alongside Astella and SoftBank. Risks: the repositioning from RPA to governance is recent and unproven in revenue (not disclosed); big RPA, cloud and security vendors can bundle governance; the Series A press does not list Norte, so follow-on is unconfirmed; the product name changed (Sentinel, Sprav) which may signal an unfinished product line.

value: Hyperplane was a data-intelligence startup that built foundation models for banks: a platform on which a financial institution could train, evaluate and deploy self-supervised deep-learning models on its own customer and transaction data, to predict credit risk, collections, churn, income or the next product a customer would buy. Instead of the regressions and gradient-boosted trees most banks use, Hyperplane's neural networks were trained on sequences of unstructured behaviour, such as click streams, transactions and text, and a bank could train hundreds of bespoke models from one hub. It was founded in Silicon Valley in 2022 (one article says 2021) by two Brazilians, Felipe Lamounier (CEO, who had worked at TOTVS and was part of the founding team of StartSe) and Felipe Meneses (the first Brazilian to win a Thiel Fellowship, who was studying at Stanford), by Daniel Silva (previously in AI at Google, described as a head at Google Brain) and by Rohan Ramanath (from LinkedIn's AI division). They chose Brazil as the first market because Brazilian banks adopt financial technology fast, and worked in stealth with three banks as design partners, which grew to about a dozen Brazilian institutions by launch; one neobank raised its credit-limit transaction volume by 46% with better income prediction. In December 2023 Hyperplane came out of stealth with a US$6 million seed (about R$30 million) led by Lachy Groom with SV Angel, Clocktower Technology Ventures, Liquid2 Ventures, Soma Capital, Latitud, Atman Capital, Crestone VC and Norte, and said it would expand to the United States. Seven months later, on 26 June 2024, Nubank announced it had acquired the company, a transaction Startups.com.br's sources say was done by share swap and whose price was not disclosed. Nubank's CEO David Vélez called the deal small for the bank but extremely strategic, saying tests showed Hyperplane's models beat Nubank's own credit-decision algorithms on the area-under-the-curve metric. The founders said they chose to bet on the bank most ready to use the technology rather than sell to many institutions. The team now works inside Nubank, and in 2025 Nubank reported training and deploying billion-parameter foundation models across several predictive use cases after eight months of work with the Hyperplane engineers.

value: Problem: banks sit on large first-party datasets (transactions, app behaviour, customer service text) but most of their predictive models still rely on tabular features and linear or tree-based models, so a large share of the signal in unstructured and sequential data is unused. Nubank's CEO says about 70% of banks' global profit pool is in credit, so gains of 5% to 15% in credit decisions are very large for a bank (his statement, Brazil Journal). Logic and why now: the 2022-2023 progress in large sequence models made it plausible to train a foundation model on a bank's own data, and the founders, from Google Brain, LinkedIn and the Brazilian ecosystem, had the technical and sales profile to deliver it. Brazil's open-finance and Pix environment (Lamounier's argument) made Brazilian banks eager, early customers. Market and share: no independent market size was found. Our own estimate, with assumptions: if about 1,000 mid-sized and large banks and lenders worldwide could pay US$200 to US$500 thousand a year for a model platform, the revenue pool is US$200 to US$500 million; a leading vendor reaching 10% to 20% of it would have US$20 to US$100 million of recurring revenue. The actual outcome was an acquisition by Nubank, a customer with more than 100 million customers and quarterly revenue above US$2.7 billion (Yahoo/TechCrunch). The price is undisclosed, so we cannot say the return. What is different: it was one of the first companies to sell foundation models trained on a bank's own data, and Nubank's tests, according to its CEO, showed an improvement over its internal models; a dozen Brazilian bank customers before launch is strong traction for a seed company. No competitors were named in the sources read. Norte's own return is not known. Risks: a narrow product that a large customer can build in-house (the reason Nubank bought it); concentration in a few Brazilian banks; and the uncertain price. This company is an exit, so the main risk for a reader is that the outcome was small and the return undisclosed.

value: Brazilian startup, born in the UK, that runs a trade-in platform for used smartphones: stores scan and value the old phone, and Doji sells it to registered buyers for a commission.
note: Baguete (2025-11-18), Brazil Journal (2025-11-17) and Startupi (2025-11-27).

value: Doji is a trade-in platform for used smartphones. Retailers, including Claro and TIM franchises, use its software to offer customers a discount or credit for the old phone as part payment; a customer or store clerk scans the device, an AI model inspects it from photos and about 300 possible defects (an earlier description says more than 70 checks), discounts only the cost of repairing each fault and checks first that the phone is not reported lost, stolen or still financed. Doji then offers the phone, in a stock-exchange-like order book, to registered buyers such as resellers, repair shops and insurers, who have said in advance how much they will pay for each model, and picks the phone up from the store. It is asset-light, charges stores no monthly fee and earns a commission of 10% to 20% on each sale; it is also launching advance-payment and financing products for buyers. Doji was founded by Fernando Montera Filho (CEO), Satyen Fakey and Bilal Khan, who met during a master's programme at Oxford. Montera, a Brazilian serial entrepreneur who sold Becommerce to Mercado Livre in 2017 and worked there until 2021 (and sold another venture, Hubsters, to CloudKitchens in 2023), was under a non-compete in Latin America, so the team started in the United Kingdom in 2021 with a consumer marketplace that priced phones like commodities, so that every iPhone in a given condition sells at one price. The idea came when he was disappointed with the dealer's offer for his car and found that used goods pass through many intermediaries. The UK business raised a US$3 million seed in November 2021 led by Canary with Norte Ventures, 1289 Capital and angels (US$800 thousand before, US$3.8 million in total), grew to about R$1.7 million of monthly revenue in the fourth quarter of 2023, but could not raise a Series A: marketplaces had high customer-acquisition cost and the UK market already had a clear winner, Back Market. After about 18 months, Doji opened in Brazil in August 2023 (RBS Ventures invested in October 2023); it closed the UK operation in January 2024, rebuilt the product as trade-in as a service in a few weeks and had its first Brazilian contracts and revenue by May 2024. In 2025 it raised about R$10 million (reported as US$2 million) in June with Positive Ventures, Niu Ventures, Seedstars, Canary, Mago Capital, Exit North Ventures and, per PEGN, Raio Capital and Norte, plus R$3 million from Indicator Capital in November. By then it served 350 stores, moved R$3.5 million of goods a month, had processed more than 50 thousand phones, had 25 people and said it grew 35% a month, aiming for breakeven and a Series A within a year.

value: Problem: Brazilians keep a large stock of phones in drawers (the CEO says about R$1 trillion, and that 80% of people never sell an old phone), phones lose about 30% of value a year, and the current ways to sell are either consumer-to-consumer (photos, descriptions, scams) or trade-in programmes at low prices run by intermediaries that force buyers to take whole lots. Logic and why now: trade-in lets the retailer sell more new phones, the consumer gets a fair price, and buyers pay a higher unit price for just the models they want, so the platform earns a commission without holding stock. Smartphone prices are high in Brazil, the official market sold 31.8 million units and R$47.7 billion in 2025 (Abinee/IDC via Tecnoblog), and the largest trade-in player, Trocafone, recently entered extrajudicial recovery (Brazil Journal, November 2025), leaving the segment without a clear leader. Market and share: our bottom-up estimate. If trade-ins and resales of used phones in Brazil reach 20% to 40% of the 31.8 million units sold new (6 to 13 million phones a year, assumption) at an average of R$600 to R$1,200 (assumption), the flow is about R$4 billion to R$15 billion; at a 10% to 20% commission the revenue pool is R$0.4 billion to R$3 billion. Doji's current R$3.5 million a month of goods is about R$42 million a year, under 1% of the low end; a 5% to 10% share of the pool would mean R$20 million to R$300 million of revenue. The CEO's R$1 trillion figure is a claim, not a market size. What is different: it is agnostic and sits in the store, working with operators and franchises, instead of buying phones itself like Trocafone, and its order-book model pays more per phone to buyers who want specific models; the founders have already built and sold two companies. Competitors named: Trocafone, Allied's Trocafy and Assurant (which buys phones from Vivo's trade-in), and Back Market in Europe. Fit with Norte: our reading is that a repeat founder who found a market and changed course quickly when the first thesis failed matches Norte's stated interest in obsessed founders, and Norte stayed with the company from the 2021 seed to the 2025 round (named in the 2021 articles and by PEGN in 2025), a follower role alongside Canary. Risks: the 2021-2023 marketplace did not scale and the company had to start again; the business depends on retail and operator partners; margin pressure if buyers or retailers integrate the same technology; and thin disclosure (no audited revenue).

value: Mecanizou is a Brazilian B2B marketplace for auto parts that connects independent mechanic workshops with parts suppliers. The workshop enters the car's licence plate and the part it needs, by app, website or WhatsApp; the company's proprietary part-identification technology, backed by a team of specialists, finds the right part among hundreds of thousands of items from many suppliers and returns, in under a minute, options with prices, brands and delivery times, and logistics partners deliver it to the workshop within hours. The workshop pays nothing to use the platform and Mecanizou earns a commission on the parts it sells; it also sets the selling price, helped by machine learning, from the prices suppliers suggest. The site also invites suppliers to join, and says that car owners can compare parts and buy with a guarantee of origin; its customers say they appreciate multi-plate carts, weekly coupons and credit terms. The company was started in 2021 by Ian Faria (CEO), who had been an executive at Kavak in Brazil, and André Simões (CTO). They visited workshops to understand their pains, noticed that the only technology mechanics used was WhatsApp, and began, in a rented house in the north of São Paulo, with a spreadsheet that produced a PDF and a test with 40 workshops and seven people. Growth in the first year was around 70% a month. In January 2022 it raised a US$4 million seed (press says led by Monashees, Alexia and H2O Capital, while LAVCA says Alexia led it). In March 2023 it raised a US$14.5 million Series A (R$76 million) led by Monashees with Alexia Ventures, FJ Labs and Dalus Capital, to expand beyond the north zone to the rest of the city, the ABC region and Guarulhos and to invest in data and part-identification technology. At that point it had more than 1,000 registered workshops, more than 200 suppliers and over 600 thousand items; by February 2024 it reported 1,200 workshops, 300 suppliers, 700 thousand parts and a waiting list of 2,000 workshops, still serving only the city of São Paulo. In 2024 it launched AIrton, its first AI assistant, to serve workshops faster on WhatsApp, and hired a former Creditas data director as head of technology and data. The company puts the national opportunity at 121 thousand workshops, 48 thousand parts stores and distributors and a potential US$22 billion of sales (its own estimate). The sources read do not give revenue, profit or news after mid-2024.

Logic and why now: a marketplace that solves the identification problem (which part fits this plate) and then offers price comparison and fast delivery attracts workshops, and the workshops' demand brings suppliers. The company charges the supplier side a commission, so workshops use it free. Smartphone and WhatsApp habits and cheap last-mile delivery in São Paulo made this possible, and AI helps catalogue and match parts. value: Osana Salud (Osana) is an Argentine healthtech that builds technology infrastructure for the health industry: instead of selling to patients, it sells to the organisations that finance and deliver care, such as health insurers, social-security funds, hospitals and pharma. Its SaaS platform, called Osana Open Health Platform, is omnichannel and meant to be integrated quickly through simple APIs with a provider's or insurer's own management systems, and it covers the whole patient journey: digital membership card, provider directory, appointment booking, video consultation, payments and billing, continuous follow-up of patients with chronic conditions, treatment adherence, e-prescription, electronic health record and digital pharmacy. The company's argument is that insurers and providers can launch new services faster and with lower development cost by plugging into a common layer instead of building and integrating many separate systems. Osana started in 2019, a few months before the pandemic, with the founder's own money, and was built by Andrés Lawson (CEO), a co-founder of the fashion e-commerce company Dafiti who left it in 2014 and also founded and chairs the Argentine Health and Technology Chamber, and Jorge López (co-founder and COO). The first step was to build alliances with providers and insurers and iterate the product, and within a few months, according to Lawson, hundreds of thousands of people were using services through its technology. In August 2021 Osana announced a US$20 million Series A led by General Catalyst, with Quiet Capital, Preface Ventures, FJ Labs, AforeVC, K50 Ventures and Addition, which with an earlier unannounced seed brought its 2021 funding to about US$26 million, billed as the largest Series A for a Latin American healthtech. At that time it said its software reached more than 6 million patients, with contracts with providers and insurers including Sanatorio Güemes and PAMI (a fund with about 5 million members), and it planned to triple its team with remote hires and open offices in São Paulo and Mexico City. By August 2022 it had more than 100 staff and commercial operations in Argentina, Brazil and Mexico, said it wanted 60% of its revenue to come from Brazil and Mexico by 2023, and named further clients such as Hospital Austral and Hominis. It was listed by CB Insights among the 150 most promising healthtechs in the world and by HolonIQ among the top 50 in Latin America, and won the Sadosky innovation award of the Argentine software chamber (CESSI) in late 2022. The company's site was republished in February 2026, so it is still operating, but the sources read give no revenue or any financing after 2021. value: Suridata is a Brazilian health-data company that helps the buyers of corporate health plans negotiate and manage them. Its customers are insurance brokers (corretoras), employers, health plan operators (including self-managed schemes and cooperatives) and hospitals. The company collects the fragmented claims data that operators send, cleans and reorganises it, audits medical bills, and returns independent reports and clinical analysis made by physicians and nurses trained in population health, so that a broker or HR team can face the operator's own numbers with its own. The pitch is that the operator always arrives at a price-adjustment negotiation with its data, and Suridata gives the buyer a counter-argument. There are three core products, offered in levels of depth: Suri Alerta (monthly monitoring of each policy's loss ratio, with alerts on usage spikes, at-risk chronic patients and high-cost cases, plus a broker dashboard and ANS benchmarking), Suri Controle (adds audit of medical bills, a clinical commentary from Suridata's physicians and negotiation-ready indicators) and Suri Gestão (the full service, which lets a broker offer active health management without a medical team of its own, with action plans, absence management, a map of the whole population, pharmacy data, annual diagnoses and monthly forecasts of hospitalisation costs). Complementary tools include a white-label portal with the broker's branding, English reports for multinational headquarters, benchmark reports, occupational-health cross-checks and in-person health assessments. The company's site and the registry say it started in 2018 (the legal company opened on 5 November 2018, in São Paulo); it runs as a 100% remote team and blogs and speaks at industry events such as the UNIDAS and CONAU congresses and AI Brasil Experience in 2026. value: Problem: in Brazil, corporate health plans are bought through brokers and negotiated each year with the operator, which has the claims data and proposes the price adjustment. In 2025 collective plans had an average adjustment of 11.15% (ANS data reported by Jornal de Brasília and Monitor Mercantil), 14.81% for contracts with up to 29 lives, and the buyer usually has no independent way to check whether the operator's loss ratio is right. Logic: a third party that cleans and audits the data, finds billing errors and cost drivers and issues clinical analysis gives the broker a concrete argument, and its own cases show reductions of about 14 to 55 percentage points in a requested adjustment. The product is sold in levels, so a broker can start cheap with monitoring and move up. Why now: persistent medical inflation (11% in 2025, per a Suridata blog post title) raises the value of cost control, and AI and data tools make data cleaning cheaper. Market and share: no independent size could be established. Our reasoning, with no figures sourced for the number of brokers or buyers: the product serves Brazil's collective health plans, which in 2025 average a double-digit annual price increase, so even a small percentage saved on a large premium base is valuable, but we could not read the number of beneficiaries, premium volume or brokers. A reasonable path is a niche software-plus-services business, not a mass-market platform. What is different: the mix of data engineering with physicians and nurses, independent reports aimed at brokers (distribution through them) and white-label portals. Competitors named by aggregators include Blue AI; other healthtechs (Axenya, HealthBit) compete for the employer's health-cost budget. Fit with Norte: our reading, which is not confirmed, is that a technical data company inside the health insurance chain, in the stage and domain Norte backs, could have been a small, network-driven investment (an aggregator lists Norte in 2023), but no readable page names Norte, so we do not rely on it. Risks: dependence on the operators' data formats and goodwill, services-heavy delivery that limits software margins, a low-visibility company with no public financing or customer count, and large brokers building their own analytics.

value: Brazilian software that lets restaurants and delivery businesses take and grow orders on their own WhatsApp channel, with an AI attendant, digital menu, loyalty and marketing tools, without marketplace commissions.

Brendi is a Brazilian software company that helps restaurants and delivery businesses sell through their own channel, mainly WhatsApp, instead of paying commissions to delivery marketplaces such as iFood. Its virtual attendant, Brenda, is an AI that answers customers at any hour, takes text and voice orders, suggests extras and sends the Pix payment link; around her the platform bundles a branded digital menu, order management and printing, WhatsApp broadcasts, a customer-recovery tool, a cashback loyalty programme, coupons, profit reports and a live view of the delivery. The website now describes a team of eleven AI agents (service, paid traffic, social media, deliveries, finance, menu and others), a 15-day free trial and plans priced by the restaurant's monthly revenue, with paid traffic sold separately; the company says it charges 0% commission per order. The story, as told on the company's own page: Daniel Frageri, now CEO, left his engineering course at ITA to help his family's bakery, saw that every delivery owner had the same problem and started Brendi as a marketing agency (paid traffic and social media) for delivery businesses. Customers arrived but manual, slow service could not keep up, the operation collapsed and the agency failed. The founders restarted from that pain and built Brenda, then grew into a full platform, and the company says active clients grew 20 times. A 2022 city-hall article says it was created by three ITA graduates in São José dos Campos, was in the Startup São José programme, had 45 delivery clients and 20 employees, had received R$650 thousand with Locaweb among its investors, and aimed at 300 clients by the end of that year. By the 2026 seed round it had 7,100 restaurants (85% in smaller cities, where delivery apps are less present), had grown processed orders from 140 thousand to 420 thousand a week in a year, reported annual recurring revenue of nearly US$5 million and a gross margin above 40%, and planned to reach 10,000 to 15,000 restaurants by year end; part of the round bought back shares from early angels. In November 2026 the company says it serves more than 9,500 restaurants, more than 70 million WhatsApp conversations and more than R$2 billion in restaurant sales, and it opened a key-accounts area for restaurant chains and franchises, with royalty and marketing-fee collection on the platform.

Delivery apps already take 58% of delivery sales (99Food/Abrasel survey) and charge commissions that the 2022 city-hall article puts at up to 30%, so a small owner gives away margin and does not own the customer relationship. Logic: the Brazilian customer already orders by WhatsApp, and an AI that answers instantly, takes the order and closes the payment turns the owner's own channel into a sales channel with no commission, while the loyalty, broadcast and recovery tools bring the customer back. Why now: cheap language models made 24-hour conversational ordering viable (the company's own story shows the earlier manual agency broke on service volume), and Pix removed the payment friction. Market and share: no independent figure for software spend exists in the pages read. Our bottom-up estimate: the company reports almost US$5 million of ARR over 7,100 restaurants, about US$700 a year (about R$330 a month) per client; if 1.5 million establishments are the ceiling, a realistic reachable base is a fraction of those that do delivery, say 100,000 to 200,000 restaurants over several years (our assumption, about 7 to 13% of establishments), which at today's price is roughly US$70 to 140 million of ARR, and more if the platform adds payments, credit and marketing spend. This is a range for Brazil only, not a forecast. Different: it sells to the smallest restaurants in smaller cities, where 85% of clients are, with an AI-first product that evolved from a failed agency, so the founders learned the service bottleneck first-hand. Competitors named in search results: OlaClick, Saipos, Delivery Direto and Kuppi; we did not compare features. value: Brazilian AI lab with a foundation model that reads a company's relational database and predicts outcomes such as default, churn and fraud, sold to banks, telecoms and marketplaces by API and batch.

Avra is a Brazilian AI lab that builds a foundation model for relational data, the tables of customers, accounts, transactions and events that sit in a company's database, and sells predictions on top of it. Instead of flattening those tables into one row per customer, as traditional models do, its model (called Avra RFM on the website) reads the database as it is, as a graph that changes over time, and predicts outcomes such as churn, default, fraud or conversion without building a new model for each question. It is delivered by API for live decisions, in batch written to the client's data warehouse, as relational embeddings that the client's own models can use as features, and through a visual workflow tool called Studio; every model is backtested on the client's history and run in shadow beside the current one before it decides anything, and each client's data and model are isolated. Revenue comes from enterprise contracts with banks, telecoms and marketplaces, supported by what the company calls forward-deployed engineers who work inside the customer. Origin: the company was started in early 2024 (registry opening 2024-02-06) by Viviane Meister, CEO, and Bruno Alano, a former OpenAI researcher, and began as an AI service for small and medium businesses, using a graph model of the Brazilian business ecosystem to score credit risk and predict customer value; it gained visibility when Nubank bought Hyperplane, the closest competitor in audience segmentation. In July 2024 it announced a US$2 million round led by MAYA Capital with Norte Ventures and Sequoia Scout, serving two large companies and testing with six more. Since then its pitch has widened from SMEs to any relational enterprise data. Its published case says a leading Brazilian bank added Avra's prediction to its SME credit-card policy and flagged 70% of future defaulters before approval while keeping 95% approval, lifting its in-house model by 4 KS points, with the bank's own risk team running the backtest; the bank is now testing it for new approvals and for recovering rejected applicants. The company publishes research notes (a three-part series on its graph foundation models, the last in August 2026), lists nine open roles in São Paulo and remote, and in November 2026 appears at the Bloomberg Línea Summit.

value: Problem: banks, telecoms and marketplaces decide on credit, fraud, churn and pricing with models trained on flat tables, although the information that matters is in who is connected to whom: a supplier that pays late, a partner's other firm entering recovery. In Brazil this is sharpest for small companies, which Sebrae counts at almost 24 million active small businesses in the last quarter of 2025, most with little history at any bank. Logic: a graph model pre-trained on the Brazilian business network can score a company from its CNPJ alone, including ones the lender has never served; the published case reports 70% of future defaulters flagged with 95% approval kept and a 4 KS-point lift over the bank's own rating (the company's own account, backtested by the bank). It sits beside the incumbent model, so the buyer takes little risk. Why now: graph neural networks and foundation-model techniques are mature, open finance and data-sharing rules enlarge the data lenders can use, and Nubank's purchase of Hyperplane showed that AI-for-credit data teams are worth buying. Market and share: no independent size for relational-AI software was found. Our estimate, labelled as an assumption: Brazil has perhaps 50 to 150 large banks, fintechs, telecoms and marketplaces that decide credit or churn at scale; at an assumed contract of US$300 thousand to US$1 million a year, winning 20 to 40 of them is roughly US$6 to 40 million of annual revenue in Brazil, with more upside in Latin America. Different: schema-agnostic pre-training on relational data, a Brazil-specific company graph, and research-grade publishing, while most rivals sell one use case. Comparables: Fundamental raised US$255 million in 2026 for a tabular foundation model (TechCrunch headline in search results, not read), which shows investor appetite for the category, and Hyperplane sold to Nubank. Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders it believes know more than Norte; Avra's founders include a former OpenAI researcher, and Norte's network of operators can open banks, which is where enterprise sales are decided (our reading, not Norte's statement). Risks: long enterprise sales cycles and concentration in a few clients; data-access and privacy rules (LGPD) over company data; strong rivals, including the banks' own teams and global labs; the pivot from SMEs to a general platform may stretch a small team.

The number of 50 to 150 enterprise buyers and the US$300 thousand to US$1 million contract are our assumptions, with no source; the revenue range is their arithmetic (20 to 40 clients x US$0.3 to 1 million = US$6 to 40 million). value: Brazilian waste-management company that runs collection, transport and final destination for businesses through one digital platform and contract, using an asset-light network of audited partners.

Musa is a Brazilian waste-management company that runs the whole chain, from collection to final destination, for businesses, through one digital platform and one contract. It started as an asset-light marketplace that connects waste generators (bars, restaurants, supermarkets, offices, industries), haulers and recyclers, with no trucks or landfills of its own: it supplies the bags and bins, trains the staff, separates waste into organic, recyclable and other, schedules daily pickups and shows the process in an app. The pitch is that 100% of the waste becomes a product or service: organics go to partners that turn them into fertiliser and, with fly larvae, into animal-feed protein, and recyclables go back to industry. Today the site presents Musa as the infrastructure that unifies the links of Brazil's waste chain: collection, transport and final destination of hazardous, non-hazardous and recyclable waste for units anywhere in the country, a network of audited partners, automatic issue and closing of the mandatory transport and final-destination documents (MTR, CDF, DMR), carbon and performance indicators, a dashboard of cost per unit, and a 30-day start (map flows, design the strategy, mobilise the partners, release the Portal Musa and train the team); the customer gets one invoice for many sites and Musa takes the margin from a better price in its network. Where it came from: Fabrício Guimarães, formerly of Philips marketing, and Martin Junck, a Frenchman, saw in a trip to Switzerland that restaurants served food on reused tableware, found that waste reuse was an undigitised sector with social impact, went through Singularity University's acceleration in Silicon Valley and started Musa in 2020 (registry opening 2020-11-13) with their own capital; later investors named in the press include Kaszek and the German fund JFC, and Lower Carbon Capital lists Musa in its portfolio. Traction told by the company: in May 2022 it launched a zero-landfill, CO2-neutralised service with Alelo for the card issuer's merchants; in December 2022 it had 130 employees, had collected more than 15,000 tonnes in Greater São Paulo and was close to operational break-even; a company profile of June 2023 gives more than 550 clients, more than 18,000 tonnes reused and more than 15,000 tonnes of CO2 avoided. In 2024 Anderson Taniguchi, formerly of Rappi operations, joined as COO and a registry administrator.

Logic: an asset-light platform that signs one contract with the generator and uses audited partners in every region gets the efficiency of a vertically integrated operator without the capital of trucks and landfills; the digital record produces the documents and the ESG numbers the customer needs. Why now: tighter regulation (reverse logistics, landfill closure) and ESG reporting make traceability a purchase criterion, and large chains want one supplier for all units. value: Brazilian software company whose AI assistant prepares meetings, records conversations in the CRM and drafts follow-ups for investment-advisory firms; it began as a WhatsApp assistant for self-employed professionals.

Assis is a Brazilian software company that began as a WhatsApp virtual assistant for self-employed professionals and now sells an AI assistant to investment-advisory firms. In its current form the product, called Assis for investment advisory, works behind the scenes of an advisor's day: before a meeting it gathers the client's history from the CRM, calendar, e-mail and WhatsApp into a short briefing and agenda; after the conversation it organises the summary, the agreements and the next steps and writes them into the CRM for the advisor to review; between meetings it prepares follow-up messages, monthly report summaries (with the original PDF from the authorised source), notices to groups of clients and referral follow-ups. Every message passes through the advisor before it is sent, and investment decisions stay with the firm. It connects to Gmail, Outlook, Google Calendar, Microsoft Teams, WhatsApp, HubSpot, RD Station and Salesforce, Google Meet is marked as coming soon, and the sales route is a diagnostic call that tailors flows to each firm. The earlier product: in April 2023 Assis announced its first round of R$27.5 million, before launching, to build a ChatGPT-based assistant for solo entrepreneurs that handled first contact, reminders, quotes, availability and charges, in a model that would earn from payment capture and a SaaS subscription; in tests, 23% of users reported higher sales. It was founded by Raphael Machioni (CEO), co-founder and former CEO of the benefits company Vee, sold to Swile in 2020; João Bergamo (CPO), former Vee CFO; and Vagner Dutra (CTO), a founding member of PicPay's technology team. When the company changed from self-employed workers to advisory firms is not stated on the pages read; the 2026 site cites a July 2025 InfoMoney report on the use of CRMs by XP advisors.

value: Problem: in Brazil an investment advisor is an independent professional who sells and follows up investments for a broker, and the value of the job is the client relationship. Advisors spend part of every day on preparing meetings, writing notes into the CRM and chasing follow-ups, and the site cites a figure from XP's head of CRM that advisors who use a CRM raise 2.5 times more, which only helps if the CRM is actually filled. Logic: an assistant that reads the calendar, mail and WhatsApp, drafts the briefing and the post-meeting record and leaves the human to approve gives the advisor hours back (the site's own simulation: 10 meetings a week x 30 minutes = 5 hours a week per advisor) and makes the CRM complete without typing. Why now: language models can summarise and draft well enough, and the advisor channel has grown: Ancord counted 27,425 accredited advisors in April 2026, with 20,087 linked to institutions, and 1,072 new ones in four months. Market and share: our bottom-up estimate: 20,000 linked advisors times an assumed subscription of R$300 to R$600 a month (assumption, no price on the page) is R$72 to R$144 million a year, or about US$13 to 26 million at R$5.6 per dollar; a strong outcome of 20 to 30% of advisors would be roughly US$3 to 8 million of annual revenue in this niche, so the thesis needs expansion to other relationship-driven professions, as the original self-employed product tried to do. Different: workflows tailored to each firm with human approval, which suits a regulated business, and a team that raised R$27.5 million before launch with prior exits from Vee and PicPay. Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders it believes know more than Norte does and brings top funds onto the cap table; the 2023 round had Costanoa, MAYA, Canaan, Latitud, FJ Labs and others beside Norte (our reading of the fit, not Norte's statement). Risks: the niche is small; the company has changed its target customer once; incumbents (CRM vendors, brokers' own tools and large AI assistants) can add the same features; advisors depend on the broker's systems and compliance rules; no public traction numbers for the new product.
note: Market: Ancord, 27,425 advisors and 20,087 linked, April 2026 (https://bpmoney.com.br/melhores-da-assessoria/brasil-ganha-mais-de-mil-novos-assessores-de-investimento-em-2026-diz-ancord/). The R$300 to R$600 monthly price and the 20 to 30% share are our assumptions; R$5.6 per dollar approximates the 2025 average in fx.csv (5.5855). Arithmetic: 20,000 x R$300 to 600 x 12 = R$72 to 144 million. The XP CRM statistic is quoted on the company site from InfoMoney (not read). value: Brazilian company, formerly Comp, that co-builds companies' HR functions with HR experts, AI engineers and custom software, covering 11 HR areas from recruiting to offboarding.

Zivo, until November 2026 called Comp, is a Brazilian company that builds a company's human-resources function with it, mixing HR specialists, AI engineers and software. Its site describes it as an AI-native HR partner: it co-builds the whole function end to end, from recruiting to offboarding (11 HR areas), with custom tools running on a layer it calls People.OS that holds all the client's people data; clients start with one or more areas and pay a monthly fee based on size and complexity, and decisions to hire, promote or dismiss stay with people. The model, which the founders call a superpowered HR teammate, places experts inside the client's routine as a right hand of the head of HR (forward-deployed). Examples on the site and in the press: Nubank uses a custom tool to prepare more than 90% of its job offers, QuintoAndar's manager satisfaction with performance reviews rose from 25% to 96%, PicPay's HR business partners build salary offers with market data inside policy, Creditas moved variable pay and long-term incentives out of spreadsheets, Dock runs a PeopleHub on People.OS and Hapvida, with more than 75,000 employees, puts its people data in one place; the site lists more than 150 clients such as Vivo, iFood, Sem Parar, Ascenty and RecargaPay. Origin: the company was founded in July 2022 in Brazil by Christophe Gerlach, an American, and Pedro Bobrow, a Brazilian, who met at Cornell, where they had built a food-delivery company that was acquired in their last year; Gerlach then worked at General Atlantic and Bobrow at Lyft, and after two years studying HR they moved to São Paulo. They began with a free salary-benchmark platform and compensation surveys, with more than 350 users and data on 70,000 employees at the time of the 2023 round, and planned to charge for salary tables and competitor analysis; later it moved into full HR services. A R$14 million first round in March 2023 was led by Kaszek with Canary, Norte and 1616 and 40 angels; in February 2026 a R$100 million Series A was led by Khosla Ventures, its first investment in Brazil, with Keith Rabois joining the board. On 17 November 2026 the company changed its name to Zivo, said AI for HR passed US$10 million in annual recurring revenue (five times in 12 months, about 85% of revenue, about 100 clients), and announced plans to enter the United States in the first quarter of 2027 with hires in New York and Miami.

value: Brazilian AI platform that forecasts demand and manages ordering and stock of fresh fruit, vegetables and greens for supermarkets and distributors, to cut waste and stock-outs.

Aravita is a Brazilian software company that uses artificial intelligence to help supermarkets and food distributors buy and manage fresh fruit, vegetables and greens (FLV in Portuguese), the products with the shortest shelf life and the most volatile demand. Its pitch is that a generic replenishment tool fails on fresh food every day, because the system's stock rarely matches what is on the shelf, so Aravita is built only for perishables. The platform corrects the FLV stock every day before ordering, forecasts demand for each store from weather, seasonality, shelf life, promotions and events, forecasts stock-outs from sales rather than from recorded stock, takes minimum display into account, supports centralised purchasing (forecast of the aggregate and distribution-centre stock), gives store managers an ordering app with alerts on likely spoilage and stock-outs, and a control panel called Farol that ranks actions for the teams (losses, stock-outs, fill rate). It describes the product as ordering as a service. The company was started in 2022 by Marco Perlman (CEO), who had founded the photo-printing company Digipix in 2004 and moved to its board in September 2022; Aline Azevedo (CPO), formerly a product manager at Loft and an IT manager at Ambev; and Bruno Schrappe (CTO), founder of SapienX. They began a pilot in early 2023 with a chain of dozens of stores around São Paulo, then raised a R$12 million seed in March 2023 led by Qualcomm Ventures and 17Sigma, with Bridge, DGF, Alexia Ventures, Big Bets and Norte, plus angels from ClearSale and ex-Locaweb and Submarino, and HiPartners, a retail-focused fund, added an undisclosed amount in July 2023. In the first year it had 30 connected stores; by July 2026 it had more than 100, a contract of two years with the São Paulo chain St. Marche and two other chains not named, a fivefold revenue increase in 2025 and a reported tripling in the first half of 2026, but it had not reached break-even and, per AgFeed, had raised only that one round. Next steps named in 2023 were other perishable departments such as bakery, deli, fish and meat counters and computer vision.

value: Problem: fresh produce is the hardest category in a supermarket. Embrapa estimates that over 40% of fruit, vegetables and greens in Brazil are wasted (AgFeed 2026), shelf life is short, and demand moves with weather and price, so buyers either empty the shelf, losing sales, or over-order and lose margin. Logic: an AI that forecasts per store and corrects the real stock daily, delivered as ordering as a service, cuts both errors; the company says the problem is the daily mismatch between recorded and real stock, which it corrects before ordering. Why now: deep-learning forecasting is feasible at store level, the founder said five years earlier it could not be done, and supermarkets have digital sales data. Market and share: Brazil's supermarket sector had sales of R$1.067 trillion in 2024 (Abras) and R$1.14 trillion in 2025 (search summary; not read). Fresh produce share and software price were not found. Our estimate, labelled as assumption: if fresh produce is 5 to 8% of sales (assumption) that is R$55 to 90 billion a year in Brazil; a vendor that charges 0.2 to 0.5% of the fresh sales of the stores it serves (assumption) earns R$110 to 450 million a year if it served all of them, so serving 10 to 20% would be about R$11 to 90 million (US$2 to 16 million) a year; adding other perishable departments and other countries widens it. This is a rough range. Different: single focus on FLV against general replenishment tools, daily stock correction, and a large-chain strategy because chains hold the best data. Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs obsessed founders and brings top funds onto the cap table; here Qualcomm Ventures and 17Sigma led and Norte took part in the seed, with a founder who built and ran Digipix for 18 years (our reading, not Norte's statement). Risks: slow sales cycles with big chains and few customers, so concentration; no break-even yet; the large replenishment vendors can add fresh-produce modules; results depend on store data quality; only one round raised, so runway may be tight.
note: Market: Abras R$1.067 trillion in 2024 (https://www.folhape.com.br/economia/setor-supermercadista-fatura-r-1067-trilhao-em-2024-equivalente-a/404785/); R$1.14 trillion for 2025 appeared only in search results. Fresh share (5 to 8%) and price (0.2 to 0.5% of fresh sales) are our assumptions, with arithmetic: R$1.14 trillion x 5 to 8% = R$57 to 91 billion; x 0.2 to 0.5% = R$114 to 456 million; 10 to 20% of that = R$11 to 91 million; at about R$5.6 per dollar, US$2 to 16 million. value: Latin American payments company that offers cross-border payments and 24/7 FX through stablecoin rails and a single API, with Mexican peso rails and market making for non-USD stablecoins.

Capa is a financial-infrastructure company, with a Mexican legal entity, that moves money between Latin America and the rest of the world using stablecoins underneath and one API on top. Its site calls it a 24/7 FX and payment platform: it receives local currency (for example Mexican pesos through SPEI), converts fiat to stablecoins and back around the clock, and settles to local bank accounts, so fintechs, payment companies, financial institutions and corporations can send and receive first- and third-party cross-border payments, hold treasury and fund local entities, all through an API, SDK or dashboard, with clients able to start transacting within 24 hours. A market-making arm provides liquidity from OTC markets, exchanges, DeFi protocols and DEXs, with a focus on keeping non-USD stablecoins, such as a digital Brazilian real and a Mexican-peso stablecoin, close to their fiat value. Customers pay through FX spreads and fees (our reading: the pages read do not state pricing). A customer quote on the site says payouts fell from 48 hours to 10 minutes and FX costs dropped by more than 60%. The company began as a crypto on-ramp and off-ramp for buying and selling crypto with Mexican pesos, founded by CEO Juan Diego Oliva (who had worked at Tools for Humanity and the Arbitrum Foundation) and CTO Juan David Torres Velasco (previously at Microsoft and co-founder and CTO of the Mexican start-up Alcancia), with a CFO and a CMO named in the press, and it announced a US$2.5 million pre-seed round in early 2025 (including a US$1 million extension) and said it operated in Mexico and the Dominican Republic and would expand to similar markets; in April 2025 it joined the Borderless.xyz stablecoin payment network to provide Mexican local rails, and in May 2025 it integrated Ondo's yield-bearing USDY so Mexican users could deposit pesos and receive dollar-denominated Treasury exposure on Solana.
