value: Problem: moving money between Latin America and the world still means slow settlement, high FX costs and a separate banking relationship in every country. Mexico alone received US$61.8 billion in remittances in 2025 (Banxico, down 4.6% from the 2024 record of US$64.7 billion), and more than 95% comes from the United States, so the corridor is large, and companies that pay suppliers, contractors or users across the region face similar friction. Logic: stablecoins settle in minutes at any hour, and a company that holds local rails and liquidity can quote competitive FX and let clients integrate once through one API; Capa says clients cut payout times from 48 hours to 10 minutes and FX costs by more than 60% (a customer testimonial on its own site). Why now: dollar and local-currency stablecoins are mainstream enough that regulated partners such as Borderless.xyz, Ondo and DFNS build on them, and a digital Brazilian real and Mexican-peso stablecoin now exist. Market and share: the 2025 remittance flow to Mexico alone is US$61.8 billion; a provider keeping 0.3 to 1% of the volume it handles (assumption, no price read) would earn US$0.2 to 0.6 million per US$100 million moved; if Capa reached 1 to 3% of the Mexican inbound flow (US$0.6 to 1.9 billion a year, our assumption) that is roughly US$2 to 19 million of annual revenue in that corridor alone, before B2B flows to other countries. Different: local rails and liquidity in Mexico, focus on non-USD stablecoins, and an API for enterprise rather than only consumer on-ramps. Fit with Norte: aggregators list Norte as an investor, but no readable source names it, so we only say that the Manifesto describes Norte as bringing the right funds and people to cap tables, which suits a crypto-infrastructure team backed by Alter, Reverie and crypto angels, led by a CEO from the Arbitrum Foundation and Tools for Humanity ecosystems and a CTO who worked at Microsoft and co-founded an earlier start-up (our reading, from their LinkedIn profiles). Risks: regulation of stablecoins and crypto in Mexico, Brazil and the United States; thin spreads and competition from Borderless.xyz-type networks, banks, Wise-style players and other stablecoin start-ups; remittance volumes fell in 2025; reliance on partners for custody and rails; the company changed positioning from consumer on-ramp to enterprise FX.

The 0.3 to 1% take rate and the 1 to 3% share are our assumptions; arithmetic: 1% x US$61.8 billion = US$0.6 billion and 3% = US$1.9 billion; at 0.3% to 1% that is US$2 to 19 million. value: Hashdex is a crypto asset manager that lets professional and retail investors hold crypto through regulated index funds and ETFs instead of buying coins directly. It was founded in 2018 by Marcelo Sampaio, a Silicon Valley veteran of Microsoft and Oracle who had been investing in crypto since 2011 and could not find a product good enough, and Bruno Caratori, a former head of risk at Gávea with a Stanford MBA; InfoMoney's account says a third founder, the Harvard-trained mathematician Thiago Costa, was part of the trio. They started in the United States but, because Brazil's regulation was friendlier, began operating there. The core idea was an index, because nobody could know which coin would win: first its own (Hashdex Digital Assets Index), replaced in 2021 by the Nasdaq Crypto Index (NCI) built with Nasdaq. In February 2021 Hashdex listed on the Bermuda Stock Exchange what it calls the world's first crypto index ETF; in April 2021 it launched HASH11 on Brazil's B3, the first crypto ETF there, which raised over R$600 million in its offering and passed R$1 billion in net assets in a week; it also has ETFs for Bitcoin (BITH11) and Ethereum (ETHE11) and mutual funds sold on platforms such as XP, BTG and Guide, with 150,000 holders in May 2021. Revenue is mainly a management fee of 1.3% to 1.5% a year (Brazil Journal, 2021); one fund charges a performance fee. In May 2021 it raised a Series A led by Valor Capital to widen the product range and go international, with the plan to triple headcount. In 2023 Brian Brooks, former Coinbase chief legal officer and acting US Comptroller of the Currency, joined the board for Valor. In March 2026 the company named Caratori global CEO, Sampaio executive chairman and Mick McLaughlin US CEO, a formalisation of a shared management model, with offices in New York, Rio de Janeiro and London. Its own site says it manages over R$6 billion in index products in eight countries as of 30 September 2026, including what it calls the first multi-asset crypto ETF in the US.

value: Isa Saúde (ISA) takes hospital-level care to the patient's home in Brazil. It began as ISA Lab, which sent independent nurses to collect blood and apply vaccines at home, with salaried "biocondutores" carrying the samples to a lab; the brothers Fernando Pares (an economist, CEO) and David Pares (a doctor, chief medical officer), serial founders who had sold the electronic-records startup AvalDoc, started it in 2017 (the date they give; other outlets say 2018 or 2019). Their father had founded the LEGO lab chain, bought by Fleury in 2008. The model works like a decentralised network: autonomous nurses and professionals, trained for several weeks (38 days of onboarding, according to the CEO), rated by patients in the app, paid more when they score well and removed when they do not. In 2021 ISA Lab raised its first round and entered seven more states; in 2022 it raised a Series A, then bought Saúde C (home care, founded in 2020), and renamed itself Isa Saúde as it moved to more complex care: urgent home care, de-hospitalisation, rehabilitation, infusions, chronic-disease monitoring and palliative care, all under what it calls a hospital at home (it compares itself to a hospital with 700 beds across Brazil). Customers are mainly health insurers (more than 25 operators in 2025; earlier Sami, GNDI, SulAmérica, Bradesco and Amil), who pay per service; the company says its costs are 40% to 70% of traditional home care or hospital stays, readmissions are under 2% against 11% in traditional home care, and it grew revenue at 98% a year over three years without disclosing revenue. By October 2025 it had more than 4,000 professionals, over 1,500 visits a day in more than 60 cities in São Paulo, Minas Gerais, Bahia and the Federal District. That month it closed a R$160 million (US$30 million) Series B led by IFC, with IDB Lab, Dalus and Endeavor Catalyst, to grow organically and buy traditional home-care companies.

value: Winnin is a cultural-intelligence software company. It analyses public video consumption on YouTube, Instagram, TikTok, Facebook and Twitch (about 2 million videos a day, according to InfoMoney in 2024) to tell brands, agencies and media companies which topics, formats, creators and communities are rising, so marketing and creative teams start from evidence. It began in 2014 inside Coca-Cola's Founders startup programme: Gian Martinez, then a creative director at Coca-Cola, started it with Carlos Camolese (COO) and Erich Oliveira (CTO), after finding that even Coca-Cola could not answer what people actually want to watch. Coca-Cola financed a seed round; ZX Ventures (AB InBev's venture arm) and the founders of the Rio fund Dynamo, as individuals, came in a later round; by mid-2020 Martinez said he had raised US$8 million. Building the platform took about five years, and revenue tripled in 2020 as Winnin Insights moved to a software-as-a-service model sold to the whole advertising industry. Customers include Google, Coca-Cola, Netflix, Meta, AB InBev, Nubank, Unilever, Nestlé, Danone and agencies; in 2024 it had 76 clients and 35% to 40% of revenue came from outside Brazil. Clients mostly pay an annual subscription. In July 2024 Winnin announced an undisclosed Series A led by Alexia Ventures and Kaszek (Coca-Cola and AB InBev left the cap table), to open a US office with a US head, strengthen leadership and push internationally; it also joined the AWS Generative AI Accelerator (US$200,000 in credits) that year. The 2025 product has three parts: Share of Attention, a metric of the share of consumer attention a brand captures within its category and country, rebuilt in 2025 to count positive attention only; ZAI, a cultural-intelligence copilot; and sentiment analysis; the 2026 site adds creative and creator briefs and territory analysis. In March 2026 it hired Guilherme Arruda, formerly of Google and General Motors South America, as VP of growth and strategic partnerships.

value: Alude is a software platform for Brazilian real estate agencies and brokers who want to work digitally, with a focus on rentals. It was launched in 2019 by three friends, Jota Junior, Alef Miranda and Alexandre Dubugras (the CEO), and went through Y Combinator's Winter 2020 batch. In its first version the platform was free for traditional agencies and automated the paperwork of a rental: background and credit checks of the tenant, document collection and validation, online signature and the purchase of insurance, which let a contract close in a day; the company earned its revenue from financial and household products sold on top, above all residential insurance and rental guarantees, and said it wanted to become Latin America's largest provider of home insurance and rental guarantee. In September 2020 it closed a US$3.3 million seed co-led by Ribbit Capital, Y Combinator, Global Founders Capital and Maya Capital with angels such as Hugo Barra and founders of Stone, VivaReal, Wildlife, Brex, Gympass, Ingresse and Plaid; at that time 150 invited agencies used it for all their rentals, with 150 on a waiting list, and the goal was 20,000 rentals in 2021. The platform also gave brokers a database of about 332,000 property owners to prospect. Today the site presents a broader operating system for agencies: more complete tenant and owner file analysis (by CPF or CNPJ in one click), rental management that automates billing, payouts and reports, e-signature with legal validity without a digital certificate, insurance issuing and a robot that scans the web for owner-posted listings so brokers can call and win the listing. It is sold by plan, with a free trial, and the company says more than 20,000 agencies use it. No later round or acquisition was found.

value: Cannect is a patient-centred healthtech for chronic conditions, built first around medical cannabis in Brazil. It was created in 2021 by Allan Paiotti, who had just left the executive directorship of Hospital Alemão Oswaldo Cruz and became CEO, and Fernando Domingues, co-founder of the telehealth company Conexa Saúde, who had the idea and became chairman, with early backing from the founders of Adventures, Thiago Maluf of Igah Ventures and two physicians. The first version, launched in August 2021 with about 200 products from a mapped portfolio of 350, solved the path that drives doctors away: the patient finds a doctor (via Conexa's teleconsultation if needed), receives a prescription, Cannect gets Anvisa's import approval (up to 10 working days; delivery averaged 25 days), buys through sellers that cannot sell directly, and delivers at home, earning a percentage of each sale; subscriptions were planned for a second stage. The startup raised more than R$1.5 million from angels, then a seed of a little over R$10 million in late 2021 and early 2022, and in 2023 a round of undisclosed size led by Supera Capital and BluStone with YaaX Capital and family offices, bringing the total to R$40 million. It bought the content portal Cannalize and the course platform Dr. Cannabis. In 2023 it passed R$50 million in transactions; by May 2024 more than 50,000 people had been treated, about 3,000 doctors were registered (of about 5,000 allowed to prescribe), about 800 curated products were listed, and a R$5 million media-for-equity deal with 4Equity was meant to fund educational media. In August 2026 the group, which says it has 100,000 patients, bought the digital pharmacy Pill (150,000 subscription customers, 17,000 medicines) to extend from cannabis to any chronic disease, with automatic refills, and it projects revenue above R$200 million by the end of 2028. value: Gabriel is a Brazilian security company that builds a private network of smart cameras for public safety. Footage and licence-plate readings go to a 24-hour intelligence centre, which validates alerts and calls the police (the data is passed to the military police for free), and which also supports investigations after crimes. In 2021 the plans started at R$199 a month; in 2026 the average ticket was about R$800 a month, from R$400 to R$20,000 for club-style condominiums. The company started in Leblon and Ipanema, raised a R$66 million Series A led by SoftBank in October 2021, entered São Paulo in December 2021 (Pinheiros and Jardins) and in January 2024 raised a R$35 million extension co-led by Astella and Qualcomm Ventures to densify São Paulo. In 2026 the company reported operating break-even after three months of positive EBITDA, growth from 4 to 45 cities in the year, about 22,000 cameras in about 8,000 buildings in Rio, São Paulo, Minas Gerais and Espírito Santo, 4 million plate readings a day, revenue up 100% in the last year and 200% the year before; in November 2026 it counted 8,500 clients, 24,000 cameras and 75 cities in five states, and took R$20 million of subsidised credit from Desenvolve SP to build a third-generation camera with two sensors and a Qualcomm chip, to describe street events in natural language and act preventively. value: Menta is a Buenos Aires company that sells payment-acceptance infrastructure as a white label. The idea is that a company which already has a network of small merchants (a bank, a large consumer-goods maker, a regional retailer, a delivery or e-commerce platform, a fintech or super-app) can offer those merchants its own card-acceptance and financial services without building a payments company: Menta supplies the SmartPOS terminals under the client's brand, a store of apps that runs on them, the processing and back office, a modular payments platform and the local integrations in each country. The terminal can carry more than payments, such as bill payment, credit, investments, crypto cash-in, loyalty programmes or even table and stock management, and clients or third parties can add their own apps. It earns a fee on each approved transaction and shares revenue with the client, so it only earns when the client does; integration is plug-and-play in about a month with no installation cost, or custom for larger clients. Its first clients were large networks in Argentina, then Mexico and Colombia, and the company says merchants adopted it easily and that it yielded nearly six times more than the solution they used before. The company was started in 2021 by three people from payments: Virginia Folgueiro (CEO, an early Google employee in Latin America who led merchant solutions at Naranja X and had to build a similar product there, which gave her the idea), Alejandro Quirno Lavalle (originally CMO, later CFO; ex-U.S. Bank, with an earlier car-leasing fintech) and Santiago Lorenzo (CTO, 20 years in payments technology, ex-Prisma and Visa). They met over a beer and cofounded Menta in December 2021, after a pre-seed of US$1.7 million led by Pear VC with Matterscale and Gilgamesh, and joined Pear's W22 cohort. In October 2022 it announced a US$6 million seed led by Base10 Partners, with Pear, Matterscale and Gilgamesh, at a reported valuation of about US$33 million, and said it would use the money to consolidate Argentina, Mexico and Colombia and to hire. By April 2024 Forbes Argentina, which named it a Promesa Forbes, reported US$23 million in billing, about 40 people, clients among banks, large retailers and big-tech firms (e-commerce, last-mile, fintechs, super-apps) and plans for Peru, Chile and Brazil; Linked API shows 54 employees on its LinkedIn page in November 2026. The company works remotely and describes itself today as the technology infrastructure that lets any company give its own payment and financial services.

value: The problem: in Latin America a large share of small merchants still lack a good way to accept cards (the CEO says two in three have no access to payment solutions, a company claim), while the companies that already serve them (banks, distributors, consumer-goods makers, retailers, marketplaces) would like a payments product but building one in-house takes more than two years, an army of developers and long regulatory processes. The logic: Menta turns that into a product they can launch in weeks under their own brand, with a terminal that becomes a platform for other services; the timing is that debit and digital payments are overtaking cash (the FIS Global Payments Report 2022, quoted by Forbes and Bloomberg Línea, projected debit cards to be the most used in-store method in 2025 with a 25.2% share). Market size, our own estimate with labelled assumptions: assume 30 large enterprise clients across Argentina, Mexico, Colombia and the next markets by a strong outcome, each deploying 50,000 terminals, with an average of US$3,000 a month per terminal and a net take of 0.3% to Menta; that is about US$9 per terminal per month, US$450,000 a month per client, US$5.4 million a year per client and roughly US$160 million a year for 30 clients. The company said US$23 million in billing in 2024 with about 40 people, so it would be at about 15% of that scenario already; a figure that mixes volume and revenue should be read with care. What is different: white label plus an app store on the terminal, multi-country with one integration, revenue share instead of up-front cost, and a team that includes people who built a merchant solution at Naranja X and ran payments technology at Prisma and Visa. Comparable companies in the region (Pomelo for card issuing, which is also in Norte's portfolio) show the infrastructure-for-fintechs thesis works at scale. Fit with Norte, our reading of the Manifesto: experienced operators who know the sector better than any investor, a round led by Silicon Valley funds (Base10, Pear) where a Latin American fund can connect customers and local operators, and early revenue. We could not confirm that Norte took part in a given round, so this fit is a reading, not a fact. Risks: the model depends on a few large clients (concentration), competition from acquirers and super-apps that give their own terminals, regulation of payment processing and, in Argentina, currency and macro volatility; and only 2022 and 2024 press exists, so the current figures are unknown.

value: Neofin is a São Paulo fintech that automates accounts receivable and collections for medium and large companies that sell on credit. Its core product is an automated collection ruler (a schedule of messages and actions) that starts before an invoice falls due and keeps going after it does, by e-mail, WhatsApp and SMS, with a different tone and next step for each debtor profile: a customer who always pays on time gets a friendly reminder, a repeat late payer gets a firmer track that can end in credit-bureau listing and protest. Around the ruler it sells a collections CRM with effectiveness reports, a WhatsApp inbox, automatic negativation and protest, extrajudicial notification, a debtor renegotiation portal and, since 2025-2026, an AI collections agent that talks to debtors on WhatsApp 24 hours a day, answers questions, sends payment slips and closes settlements. The platform plugs into the customer's ERP and bank files through an open API and a long list of integrations (TOTVS, SAP, Sankhya, Omie, Nomus and the main Brazilian banks), and has a partnership with Serasa for credit analysis and negativation. Customers are in education, distribution, accounting, industry, occupational health, telecom and securitisation funds; named cases include Unifecaf, Contabilidade Pinheiro, Bebidas Nude, BHub (which recovered 4.9 times more value after due date within two months, by the case page) and the Loja do Mecânico. It sells software on subscription plus usage, to companies, so it is B2B. Neofin was founded in January 2023 by Laura Camargo (CEO, ex-Pátria and General Atlantic; Latamfintech adds Gympass and Inventa), Arthur Cunha (CFO, ex-Credit Suisse and iFood/Movile) and Leandro Sarmento (ex-IBM and Empiricus), who each saw finance teams chase late payments by hand, in spreadsheets, over more than 14 years of combined work in finance; the first people to back it were angels Cesar Carvalho (Wellhub, formerly Gympass) and Patrick Sigrist (iFood and Nomad). In February 2025 it announced a R$35 million seed round led by Quona Capital and Upload Ventures with 17Sigma, 1616 Ventures, Far Out, BFF, Norte and Canaan, described as one of the largest seed rounds for a Brazilian fintech founded by a woman; at that time it had about 300 clients, processed about 80,000 collections a month and had 53 employees, and planned to quadruple its client base within 2025. The money was for a fully automatic renegotiation portal, an advanced collections CRM and the WhatsApp AI agent, plus hiring in data, machine learning and AI. By April 2026 the company said more than 55% of interactions were solved without a human and that clients recovered over 50% more credit, and its site now claims more than 1,000 companies.

value: The problem: Brazilian companies that sell on credit (invoices, boletos, tuition, subscriptions) still chase late payers with spreadsheets, a few generic e-mails and a person on the phone, which is costly, embarrassing for both sides and slow, while default is high: Serasa figures quoted in the trade press put overdue debt in Brazil at R$382 billion and about 30% of companies as listed as defaulters. Founders who lived this as finance leaders (Laura Camargo as a finance director) built the product. The logic: collection is a repetitive, rule-based, multi-channel conversation that fits software and now language models well. Brazil has the data rails (ERP and bank-file integrations, boletos, Pix) and the channel (WhatsApp is where debtors answer), so an AI agent that reads the open invoices, offers terms and closes an agreement cuts cost per collection and lifts recovery; Neofin reports over 50% more recovery and more than half of interactions solved without a human (company claims). Market size, our own bottom-up estimate with labelled assumptions: assume about 300,000 Brazilian medium and large companies that sell on credit and could buy a collections platform, at an average of R$1,500 to R$3,000 a month (R$18,000 to R$36,000 a year) gives roughly R$5 to R$11 billion a year in software spend; a strong outcome of 3% to 5% of that is about R$150 to R$550 million of annual revenue. The company counts 300 clients in early 2025 and 1,000 or more on its site, so it is still near 0.3% of that count. Credit-recovery fees or usage on top would enlarge it. What is different: it focuses on the pre-due and post-due ruler with deep ERP/bank integration instead of being a debt-buying collector, it combines Serasa data with the AI agent, and it sells to mid-market companies that are too big for spreadsheets and too small for a call-centre vendor; partners such as Nomus (an ERP that already had a basic ruler and chose to plug Neofin in) show the integration route. Why it fits Norte, our reading of the Manifesto: highly intelligent, obsessed founders with direct finance experience, a round led by top funds (Quona, Upload) where Norte is a follower and can add its network of operators and angels (the angels Cesar Carvalho and Patrick Sigrist are from the same Gympass/iFood circle), and revenue from early on. Risks: ERPs and banks can add their own collection modules (the Nomus case shows ERPs already ship basic rulers), WhatsApp policy and cost changes affect the main channel, regulation of collection practices, and the market for software seats among mid-sized companies is fragmented, so growth depends on partner channels; the press reports are mostly the company's own numbers.

value: Decade is a São Paulo wealth-advisory company that pairs a proprietary investing AI with human advisors, aimed first at wealthy Brazilians who have built assets but get no private-bank-style advice. The client connects bank and brokerage accounts through Open Finance (or uploads statements and describes assets that do not show up, such as property or investments abroad), and Decade consolidates everything into one view by asset class, geography and risk, with the fees and the inner composition of each fund. It then diagnoses the portfolio (concentration, expensive products, tax inefficiency, mismatch with the client's goals), watches the market and the client's spending around the clock and raises alerts, lets the client chat with the AI to run simulations and compare investment theses, and gives each client a dedicated advisor on WhatsApp or video. The pitch is the service that multi-family offices and private banks give to the ultra-rich, without the commissions and product-pushing that the founders say distort Brazilian advice (it calls the category a 'Inteligência Patrimonial'). It makes money from a subscription of R$200 a month for the platform, the AI and advisor support, plus a by-invitation fee-based product for clients with R$5 million or more onshore and offshore, which competes with multi-family offices; it has integrations with BTG Pactual, XP, Genial and C6, and operates under a CVM investment-advisory licence while its asset-management arm (Decade Asset Management) is in the process of CVM accreditation, which would allow managed portfolios and, later, executing orders. The company was founded in September 2025 by Vitor Olivier (CEO), one of Nubank's first engineers, who built the NuConta, ran the business in Brazil and then operations and became CTO before leaving in August or September 2025, and Felipe Meneses (head of AI), the first Brazilian Thiel Fellow and cofounder of Hyperplane, the credit-AI company Nubank bought in August 2024; they met at Nubank after that deal and began talking about using AI in finance. The startup was first named Frontier Technologies. Why now: Open Finance, the Pix generation's digital habits and, above all, capable AI, which is the 'new technology wave' that Olivier says matched Nubank's smartphones-and-cloud moment. value: Flow, which trades as FlowCredi, is a São Paulo marketplace for credit backed by property (home equity), plus real-estate financing and credit backed by a vehicle. The customer enters the type of property and the amount, and FlowCredi's specialists compare offers from a network of banks and credit funds (the site says more than 20 institutions, the CEO said 14 players were integrated in November 2026) and guide the person through the process; rates quoted on the site start at 1.09% a month for home equity (up to 240 months and up to 60% of the property value), 11% a year for real-estate financing (up to 420 months and 80% of the value) and 1.79% a month for vehicle-backed credit. It serves consumers directly and also companies, and it has been building white-label channels with partners in education (medical schools, so that families can pay tuition with a property-backed loan), health (loans to clinics for equipment and to patients for procedures) and architecture (renovations), testing about 12 channels in which home equity is not normally sold. FlowCredi is paid on the credit it places, funded mainly by credit-rights funds (FIDCs) and real-estate funds. The team behind it ran Credihome, a real-estate credit marketplace founded in 2017 by Bruno Gama, Caio Alfano and Deivid Bastos and acquired by Loft in 2021; Alfano and Bastos started FlowCredi in 2024, with former Credihome executives Rodrigo Gordinho and Mayle Vaz in the leadership, and Bruno Gama took over as CEO in late 2025 (Startupi calls all four of Bastos, Gordinho, Vaz and Alfano founders, while Startups.com.br and LatamList name Alfano and Bastos). The thesis is that home equity, which they put at about R$10 billion in 2024 and R$11 billion in 2025, can grow ten times or more as the Legal Framework for Guarantees (2023, which allows the same property to back more than one loan) matures, much as real-estate credit went from R$5 billion to more than R$230 billion a year. In December 2025 it announced a R$3.5 million pre-seed co-led by Verve Capital and Norte Ventures with angels Patrick Sigrist, Rafael Duton, Leandro Abreu and Gabriel Lacombe, having approved more than R$500 million of home-equity credit in 2025 with a team of 31. In April 2026 it hired a CFO (Rafael Rodrigues Lopes) and a head of new channels (Denis Senhorini); in the first half of 2026 business owners were 32.1% of home-equity contracts, up from 14.9% a half-year earlier; and by November 2026 it said it had passed R$100 million in home-equity operations in 2026 and received more than 10,000 leads a month. The CEO also warns that costs can reach 25% to 30% a year with indexers and insurance, so the product suits people who can settle fast, not people reorganising debt.

value: The problem: Brazilians pay some of the world's highest rates on cheque especial, cards and personal loans while many own a paid-off property that could secure credit at 1.5% to 1.8% a month with terms up to 20 years; most borrowers have never heard of home equity, the product is complex and each lender asks for different documents. The logic: a marketplace that compares lenders and handles the process makes the cheaper product easy to buy, and partnerships in education and health put the offer at the moment of need (tuition, surgery, renovation). Why now: a high Selic that widens the gap versus unsecured credit, the 2023 Legal Framework for Guarantees (the same property can back more than one loan), and funding from FIDCs and real-estate funds. Market size: the press quotes about R$10 billion of home equity originated in 2024 and R$11 billion in 2025, with a sector projection of up to R$500 billion (a company-quoted figure, not independent), against more than R$230 billion a year of real-estate credit. Our estimate with labelled assumptions: if home equity reaches R$50 billion a year in Brazil within five to seven years (an assumption that is far below the R$500 billion projection), a marketplace that places 5% of it originates R$2.5 billion a year and, at a 2% to 3% placement commission (assumption, not sourced), earns R$50 to R$75 million of revenue; at the company's R$500 million approved in 2025 the same commission gives R$10 to R$15 million. What is different: founders who already built and sold a credit marketplace (Credihome to Loft), a distribution strategy based on partners outside the traditional channel and a white-label offer, and a broker model that does not carry credit risk on its balance sheet. Fit with Norte, our reading of the Manifesto: repeat founders with a track record in the sector, an early round co-led with Verve where a connector adds angels and top funds, and revenue already flowing; Norte co-led the pre-seed, which is an earlier stage than most of its follow-on positions. Risks: as a broker it depends on lenders' appetite and on FIDC funding, competition from Creditas, Bcredi and bank channels (the team's own résumés list Bcredi and Pontte as competitors), take-rate pressure as lenders go direct, and the consumer risk that the CEO himself highlights (total costs up to 25% to 30% a year, danger when used to reorganise debt), which could bring regulatory scrutiny. Confidence low because the market size is a company-quoted projection plus assumptions.

value: Brazilian fintech with an AI agent that guides people, mainly in income classes C and D, through credit: it finds the offers they can really get from partner lenders and follows the loan to the end. It is paid by lenders, not by users.
note: NeoFeed (2026-04-13), Let's Money (2026-04-14) and Startups.com.br (2026-08-25).

value: Aro is a Brazilian fintech that puts an AI agent between consumers and lenders. Instead of listing twenty offers on a marketplace, the agent talks to the user (in the app or on WhatsApp), reads their situation through open banking and behavioural data, finds out which lenders would really approve them, and follows the loan through to the end: it collects documents, checks employment from official sources, does biometrics and, if the person is in debt, shows what is blocking credit. The product covers payroll-deducted loans (consignado CLT), personal loans, loans backed by the phone as collateral and credit for people with a negative record, and it is aimed mainly at income classes C and D, who need the most guidance. The user pays nothing. Aro earns from the lender side, with three sources: a distribution fee, payment for data, and other technology services sold to lenders, including correspondent banks that were outside the big marketplaces and now get an approval pipeline of about four hours. It was created in August 2024 by Pedro Milanez, Nubank's first employee and co-founder of the proptech Lastro, and Yuri Mannes, a former vice-president of innovation at BR Media Group. The MVP went live between November and December 2025 (the press gives both months), the company left stealth on 13 April 2026 with a US$2.5M pre-seed led by ONEVC and 17Sigma with Norte Ventures, Gilgamesh and Grão VC, and by then it had passed 100 thousand users and had lent more than R$2 million from its own cash (tickets of up to R$200, using Celcoin's banking licence). By late August 2026 it reported 600 thousand registered users, about 40 integrated lenders, 200 thousand people arriving each month with growth entirely organic, annualised revenue of US$1 million (target US$3M to 4M by year end) and originations that had gone from R$100 thousand a month in December 2025 to a goal of R$10M to 15M a month by December 2026. The company dismantled its own lending book in a carve-out because it conflicted with its role as a neutral agent. Next come three embedded-finance contracts with third-party platforms (one with a benefits company), a possible new round abroad in early 2027, and, in 2027, insurance, accounts, payments, card management and agentic payments.

The press differs on the start of operation (NeoFeed: MVP in November 2025; Startups.com.br: began operating in December 2025). Revenue and user figures are company figures.

value: The problem: Brazil has 84.2 million adults with overdue bills (51.1% of adults, R$597.4 billion in debt in September 2026, Serasa), and in the same month finance companies passed utilities as the second-largest source of overdue debt. These people, mostly in classes C and D, face a crowded and confusing supply of loans, are often refused, and have no equivalent of the private banker or advisor that exists in investing; the founders call credit the main pain in the financial relationship. Today they are served by marketplaces that show many offers few of which are approved, by bank correspondents, or by nobody. The logic: an agent that works for the user, reads open-banking data, knows each lender's rules and carries the person through contracting can lift approval and cut the friction that lenders pay to remove. Lenders pay for qualified, pre-verified demand, so the user pays nothing, which avoids the problem that earlier personal-finance apps (Guiabolso is the example the co-founder gives) had in charging users. Why now: cheap language models make a conversational advisor possible at class C and D scale, open banking supplies the data, and Pix lets money reach the user at once. Market size and reachable share (our estimate): in Brazil, 84.2 million people have overdue debts and many more borrow. If 5% of that group contracted one loan a year (4.2 million loans) at an average ticket of R$3,000 (our assumption), the annual flow would be about R$12.6 billion; a distribution fee of 3% to 5% (our assumption, in line with commission practice) would be R$380 to 630 million a year of revenue pool for distributors in that segment alone, before data and software fees and before insurance and payments. The company's own goal of R$10M to 15M a month by December 2026 would be under 1.5% of that flow; a strong outcome of 5% to 10% share is plausible only if lender coverage grows well beyond 40. What is different: it sits on the user's side but is paid by lenders, it integrates correspondent banks that marketplaces skip, it keeps the user to the end of the contract, and it sells technology services to lenders. Growth has been fully organic, reaching 600 thousand registered users in about eight months. Fit with Norte (our reading, not Norte's statement): Norte says it backs obsessed founders who know more than it does, builds on a network and adds value by connecting the right people and bringing funds to the cap table. Aro's founder said he chose the pre-seed investors because the business will need funding, and wants credit-specialist funds next; connecting a first-time-fund-raiser to credit funds and to lenders is where a network helps. Risks: dependence on a few lender partners and on their approval rules; credit quality in the C and D segments and the reputational risk of showing rates up to 22% a month (the site discloses them); regulation of correspondents and of data use; incumbents (large marketplaces, banks' own apps) copying the agent; and the unproven claim that AI guidance improves repayment, which the Let's Money piece also flags.

Our arithmetic: 84.2M x 5% = 4.2M loans; x R$3,000 (assumption) = R$12.6B; x 3% to 5% fee (assumption) = R$380M to R$630M. Aro's R$10M to 15M a month x 12 = R$120M to 180M, which is 1% to 1.4% of R$12.6B. Confidence low because ticket and fee are our assumptions and no independent market-size report was read. value: Fly Media (written FlyMedia in the press) is an AI-native media company that creates synthetic influencers and characters and treats each one as an intellectual property (IP) that can be scaled globally, in the way Disney treats its characters. The characters are built with AI from their personality to the content they publish, are multilingual from birth, and are meant to run across platforms with a small team: the CEO says that one AI influencer lets the company make 100 creatives for a brand in a day, against about 10 for a human creator. The company says it does not sell hours of video or custom avatars to brands, because that would put a ceiling on the business; its main customer is the audience (B2C), with brand partnerships, licensing (notebook covers, the education sector) and communities as the way the IPs make money. Its site presents an internal production platform, Fly Studio, that takes a character from script to storyboard to finished video and feeds each piece's performance back into the character's profile; Fly Hub, a Discord community where AI creators take classes on virality and compete in paid championships; and a counter of cumulative views across its IPs (the site says more than one billion views and more than ten original IPs; these are company figures that change in real time). The founder is Victor Trindade, known as Eagle, who co-founded the Neagle and FOCO channels (23 million followers and over 5 billion views by his account), the influencer agency FANSTAR in 2021 and the Gen Z fintech NG.CASH, where he worked with Mario Augusto Sá, who is a co-founder of FlyMedia. In April 2026 he said the company had been an influencer agency for about ten years and an incubator of human creators, which he found unreliable because he could not control creators' motivation; the lesson led to the AI IP model. FlyMedia launched on 11 December 2025 with a R$20 million (about US$3.7 million) seed led by ONEVC with Big Bets, Alter Global, the a16z Scout Fund, Norte, Hypersphere, Verve, FJ Labs and individual investors including Fersen Lambranho. By April 2026 its first two characters had traction in under two months: Zuka, a talking football that reached 500 thousand followers in 40 days with no paid media and whose world also became a map in Fortnite, and Foka, an animal character who explains the conversations of X, launched a week after Big Brother Brasil 26 began and reached 60 thousand followers on Instagram. The money is meant to develop the first AI influencers, narrative universes and digital brands for several markets.
note: Pages used: Forbes Brasil 2026-04-20 (Zuka, Foka, the ten-year agency history, 100 creatives, brand stance), Forbes Brasil 2025-12-11 and Startups.com.br 2025-12-11 (round, investors, founders, NG.CASH and FANSTAR), Let's Money 2025-12-11, LatamList 2025-12-12 and the site flymedia.ai (Fly Studio, Fly Hub, views counter). Views, followers and creative counts are company figures.

value: The problem: creator-led media is hard to scale and hard to control. A human creator tires, changes goals, carries reputational risk and can leave; the founder's own agency and incubator, which spent about ten years and a lot of energy training creators, found that stability and delivery could not be guaranteed. Brands, on the other side, want large volumes of creative at low production cost. The logic: generative video, image and voice models make it possible to build a character with a defined personality and produce its content in volume, in several languages, and to own the resulting IP instead of renting a person's attention. Why now: model quality has crossed the threshold at which synthetic characters can hold an audience (Zuka reached 500 thousand followers in 40 days according to Forbes), and short video is a cheap funnel to long-form watch time, which the CEO says is the metric he optimises. Market size and reachable share: the Forbes pieces quote a Grand View Research figure of about US$50 billion for synthetic influencers by 2030 and a projected creator economy of US$480 billion by 2027; both are second-hand figures from reports not read, so they are leads. A bottom-up sketch, with every input our assumption: if ten IPs each reached 5 million followers and earned US$0.50 per follower per year from licensing, brand deals and products, revenue would be about US$25 million a year; a breakout IP of the kind that Disney-style franchises produce is worth far more, but it is a power-law outcome, not a base case. A realistic strong outcome is a global brand portfolio in the tens of millions of dollars of annual revenue, not a share of the whole creator economy. What is different: it is a studio for owned AI IPs rather than a tool or an agency, it comes from a founder who has already built audience (Neagle, FOCO), an agency and a fintech with seven million users, and it has an internal production pipeline (Fly Studio) and a creator community (Fly Hub). value: BOND is a São Paulo startup that uses AI to run the operations of accounting. It began, in the April 2026 press, as a full-service accounting firm for small and mid-sized companies with annual revenue between R$3.6 million and R$50 million: for the complex, high-touch cases a human accountant serves the client, with about ten times more reach thanks to AI tools, and for routine work (payroll, tax slips, a dismissal simulation that takes a traditional firm days and BOND minutes, instalment of an overdue Simples slip) everything is automated. Its current site presents a second shape: a partnership for accounting offices, in which BOND takes over the operation (team, systems and office space) of an existing firm while the firm keeps its clients, brand and advisory work. BOND says the software closes the month in about one hour, answers employees' payslip questions by voice or text with a human review before it is sent, checks each client's tax position at the Receita through Serpro and the client's certificate, and converts data from the main accounting ERPs (Domínio, Questor, Contmatic, SCI, Alterdata). The offer is for firms with monthly recurring revenue from R$40 thousand and promises to keep the firm's margin, with BOND earning from scale; the press says it was also considering buying client portfolios from traditional firms. The date of the shift from direct service to the partner model is not public. The founders are Matheus Oliveira, an early Loft employee who then worked at the family office FitPart and founded his own manager, FW Capital, in 2022, and Gabriel Jordão, who spent 14 years at Jusbrasil as a programmer and then product director. They say the sector is highly fragmented (more than 100 thousand offices), uses ERPs from the 2000s and has ageing owners with no succession plan, and that startups such as Contabilizei and Agilize serve micro-businesses but not mid-sized ones. The company was created in about December 2025 (it was four months old in April 2026), opened its Brazilian entity in February 2026, and announced on 15 April 2026 a round of R$10 million (about US$2 million), led by Propel with Kiara, Norte Ventures, Hypersphere and the iFood co-founder Patrick Sigrist. At that point it served ten beta clients and was about to start selling.

value: The problem: Brazil has more than 100 thousand accounting offices (101,880 registered organisations, with a 40% increase between 2020 and 2025, according to a benchmark reported by Sitecontabil), and 79% of them have no structured sales area. Most are small, run by ageing owners with no succession plan, work on old ERPs and spend very little on technology; their clients, especially companies with R$3.6M to R$50M of revenue, get slow service and often pay more tax than necessary. The logic: accounting, payroll and tax compliance are rules-driven, document-heavy and repetitive, a good fit for software plus human review. By operating the back office of many offices on one stack, BOND can lower unit cost and keep the office owner's margin while giving the client faster service. The new partner model also solves its own distribution problem: instead of winning thousands of SME clients one by one, it takes over books of business through offices that already have them, and offers owners a succession route. Why now: language models read documents and talk to employees reliably enough to automate most tickets, and the tax reform adds complexity that offices struggle to handle. Market size and reachable share (our estimate): Sebrae reports 3.93 million new small businesses opened from January to August 2026 (Agência Sebrae). Take the roughly 100 thousand offices as the channel. If a typical office has R$40 thousand to R$150 thousand of monthly revenue (the company's minimum is R$40 thousand; the upper figure is our assumption), the sector's yearly billing is on the order of R$50 to 180 billion; our share assumption is that BOND operating 1% to 3% of offices at an average R$80 thousand a month would be R$0.96 to 2.9 billion a year in managed revenue, of which BOND keeps the part that is not paid back to the offices (its fee is not public). This is a rough order of magnitude, not a market report. What is different: it is a service business built on its own software rather than a tool sold to accountants, it positions AI as a way to make fewer errors rather than to cut cost, and the founders combine product (Jusbrasil) with finance and real-estate operations (Loft, FW Capital). Fit with Norte (our reading, not Norte's statement): Norte says it backs obsessed founders and adds value by connecting the right people and bringing top funds and angels onto the cap table. A first round led by Propel, with Hypersphere, Kiara and an iFood co-founder alongside Norte, matches that pattern; a service roll-up needs funding, introductions to office owners and hiring help, areas where a network helps. Risks: service quality and liability when AI makes a tax error; the transition of clients between offices is operationally heavy; unit economics are unknown and the company has few clients (ten at announcement); acquiring portfolios needs capital; the pivot between two models in months shows the model is still being found; and incumbents (Contabilizei, Agilize, ERP vendors) may add AI.

value: Maggu AI is a Brazilian startup that gives pharmacy counter staff an AI copilot. Most attendants are not pharmacists and, after interviews with more than 100 of them, the founders found that they could not answer more than two questions about most products; the Maggu system plugs into the pharmacy's management software and, in real time and inside the normal sales flow, tells the attendant how a product is used, what care it needs (for example, avoiding the sun after an acid anti-wrinkle treatment), which complementary items fit and what to explain, which supports pharmaceutical attention and raises basket size and customer satisfaction. Its knowledge base holds technical data, package inserts and information on more than 1.6 million products sold in Brazilian pharmacies. The offer is plug and play: the pharmacy keeps its systems and adds the layer on top. The company was created in 2023 by Felipe Trevisan and Luiz Andrade, with co-founders Pedro Magela, Reslley Gabriel and Rérica Lins; Magela and Gabriel had created and sold parts of startups before (SnackIn, an autonomous-market company whose operation was partly bought by Shopper), another partner sold a company to Infracommerce, and Lins comes from pharmacy retail. It raised an undisclosed pre-seed in 2024 from Latitud and Airborne Ventures. In 2025 it grew its customer base about twenty times, mainly among small and mid-sized independent pharmacies, which adopt new technology faster. On 9 March 2026 it announced a R$22 million seed led by DGF Investimentos with Norte Ventures and IC Ventures as new investors and follow-on from Latitud and Airborne, at a R$138 million valuation and more than R$28 million raised in total. It was connected, through system integrations, to about 17.5 thousand pharmacies, of which 2.2 thousand were actively using the platform and the rest were in technical activation. The plan stated then: about 500 pharmacies added a month, rising to about 2 thousand a month by year end; close the first large chain contract within 30 to 60 days; near 30 thousand pharmacies actively using the platform by the end of 2027 (about 30% of Brazilian pharmacy retail, by the founder's account); a Series A in 2026; and a possible first pilot in Mexico at the end of 2027, since Latin America has close to 270 to 300 thousand pharmacies.

value: The problem: pharmacy is Brazil's first point of contact with the health system, but the counter is staffed by high-turnover attendants who cannot know thousands of products; management systems are mostly transactional. Independent pharmacies are the majority by count and the company's first customers. The logic: a language-model copilot fed with product and clinical content and integrated into the existing system gives each attendant the knowledge of a pharmacist at no hardware cost, and the pharmacy pays because basket size, cross-sell and customer experience improve. Why now: model quality, plus 2026 changes in the sector (a March 2026 law allows pharmacies inside supermarkets and pharmacy clinical services are growing) raise the value of good counter service. Market size and reachable share: the Medicina S/A page reads about 93 thousand pharmacies and drugstores in Brazil in November 2026 (net margin of the large listed chains between 1% and 3%), and Abrafarma ranks the largest chains at R$118.5 billion of revenue in 2025 with 11,688 stores across associated chains (Mercado & Consumo). Our estimate of the independent pool is therefore on the order of 80 thousand stores. If a store paid R$300 to R$500 a month for the copilot (our assumption, not disclosed), 30 thousand stores would be R$108 to 180 million a year in Brazil; a large-chain contract would be worth more per customer. A realistic strong outcome is 20% to 30% of Brazilian pharmacies, which is what the company's own target implies. Latin America would add up to about three times the store count. What is different: it is a vertical copilot at the point of sale, integrated into the management system rather than a chatbot app; it already has 17.5 thousand integrations, the team has operated retail and pharmacy before, and nine of ten owners reportedly close at the first conversation (company claim). Fit with Norte (our reading, not Norte's statement): Norte says it backs obsessed founders and adds value by connecting people and bringing top funds to the cap table. A seed led by DGF (a software specialist) with Latitud and Airborne already on the table, and a founder team made of repeat entrepreneurs, is the sort of syndicate in which a follower role is natural. Risks: only about 2.2 thousand of 17.5 thousand connected stores use the product, so conversion and retention are the main unknown; pharmacy margins are thin and independents are under pressure; chains may build their own AI or buy from system vendors; the pricing is not disclosed; and the quality and liability of health advice from AI require review and regulatory attention.

value: Core AI is a São Paulo company that lets software companies, marketplaces and other businesses offer credit to their own customers without building a lending operation. It positions itself as the intermediate layer between the end client and banking-as-a-service providers such as Celcoin, QI Tech and Stark Bank: those providers supply the ability to lend, but not the expertise to analyse data and build the best credit model, so the company builds the whole credit pipeline for the client using AI and the behavioural and transactional data the client already holds (a real-estate software firm, for example, has years of rental payment data). The site lists four building blocks: receivables anticipation embedded in the client's product, a white-label credit platform ready to operate, a connection to the credit market for funding, and AI models that estimate default, set limits, rates and conditions for each customer, detect fraud and run collections with a multi-agent system by voice, WhatsApp and email. Clients connect by API or use the white-label product; the models are tuned on the client's own data. The company says it can set up a credit pipeline in under a month, and it earns a mix of a fixed take rate and a share of results. It was founded in 2025 by Enrico Francesco Damiani and Fernando Martins, who have worked together for more than eight years: they met at university, when Martins founded an HR-tech, Preparo, that helped companies hire interns, and Damiani was its first employee; after selling it they led data science, analytics and machine learning at Stone. NeoFeed also names Carolina da Costa Carvalho as a founder, with an MBA from Columbia. They started from the shared pain that credit was hard to get in Brazil. In July 2025 it announced a pre-seed led by Big Bets (US$1 million, according to NeoFeed; Brazil Journal later says a US$400 thousand round came right after its creation) with angels including Daniel Silva of Hyperplane, Fersen Lambranho of GP and Lívia Kuga, ex-Stone. It was already working in real estate and health, with rent anticipation for landlords and receivables anticipation for doctors, with more than 40 thousand active users, 70% of the base pre-approved, default below 1% and credit released in seconds (company figures), funded by family offices and angels. On 19 March 2026 it raised a US$4.1 million seed led by 14B (one of the managers that came out of the split of Upload Ventures) with Big Bets, Norte Ventures, Nameless and the New York manager BFF and the Stone founders André Street and Eduardo Pontes as angels. value: Datamint is a Rio de Janeiro company that builds an AI platform to manage physical assets in critical industrial operations such as oil and gas, energy, sanitation, heavy industry and, as targets, pharmaceuticals, steel and cement. The system ranks maintenance by consequence for the operation instead of queue order, decides maintenance, parts and logistics together, and records each intervention as traceable evidence for audits and regulators. A key difference is what it calls auditable AI: it combines AI models with deterministic systems, operational rules and mathematical optimisation so that every recommendation can be traced, explained and verified, which matters in regulated sectors where generative models alone are not enough. It runs on top of existing systems without replacing them, and uses partners' technology such as Google and Nvidia and databases such as Neo4j and Redis. value: Oasis (Oasis HQ, at joinoasis.com) is a New York software company that sells a shared workspace where people and AI teammates work together. Its argument, set out on its About page, is that AI agents arrive like rookies with talent but no chemistry: they do not know a team's norms, so they create drag, overspend and lose context when the team switches models or tools. Oasis is the place where they can learn from the work itself. The product combines rooms (group chats where people and agents share context and co-edit documents, sheets or code), a shared memory that carries what the team has learned across any model or harness, roles and permissions per agent (View, Use, Edit or Admin), approval rules for actions such as sending an email, recurring scheduled work, reusable instructions and skills, per-agent budgets that connect spend to projects, tasks and outcomes, and a choice of models from those the organisation approves. Teammates log into the tools the team already uses (for example Salesforce) with their own computer and browser, and the company says its agreements with model providers prohibit training on customer data and that a DPA covers each customer. Example agents on the site do sales prospecting, follow-up of commitments made in calls, and campaign suggestions. The company is led by ex-Palantir forward-deployed engineers, who say they have deployed agent systems in the real world: Stefano Fantini Delmanto is the CEO and Naveen Sharma, with a background in AI, robotics and applied mathematics, is a founder; blog posts are signed by Stefano, Naveen and Jayson. Market (rough, assumption-based, no independent size was read): the company says WhatsApp has 3 billion users and that it has 28,000 developers. If 1,000 teams paid US$200 to US$500 a month that is US$2.4M to US$6M a year; 10,000 such teams would be US$24M to US$60M, before any share of message volume if it resells Meta messages. value: Kayro sells artificial intelligence for the commercial operation of manufacturers (consumer-goods industries), distributors and wholesalers in Brazil. Its premise is that sales teams in these companies spend their time on operational tasks, act as order takers and receive confusing guidance, while WhatsApp has become one of the main sales channels with no visibility for the company. The product has several parts. For the field salesperson it crosses the company's own data and gives hyper-personalised direction on what to do at each point of sale, with the argument behind the recommendation, and organises the day (what to do, in which order, at which stores). For order intake, the list that arrives by WhatsApp comes back as a quote with the items identified and the company's commercial conditions applied, and orders in PDF, Excel and other formats enter the sales-force system without retyping. It also matches the point of sale's sell-out with the manufacturer's sell-in to warn when a product is about to run out at the customer, sends commercial offers only to the right customers, and turns salesperson-customer conversations into indicators (service level, what is won and lost). A separate product, the Sales Copilot (Copiloto de Vendas), puts an assistant inside the team's WhatsApp so salespeople ask questions in natural language, managers receive reports and alerts about drops in performance, upsell and churn, with integration to ERPs, CRMs and spreadsheets. The company supports two teams in one operation, street sellers and telesales, and says telesellers become ten times more efficient. Data is captured by API, direct database connection, data lake or file export; each customer's data is separated at database level, is not used to train Kayro's own models and is handled under the LGPD; each customer has an engineering and business team and a customised deployment. Kayro is based in Jardim Europa, São Paulo, and has three co-founders, all early in their careers. Antonio Matarazzo Affonso Ferreira is the CEO; before Kayro he founded and sold WebHorse, a marketplace for show-jumping horses that, by his own account, connected R$3.5 million of horse sales in two years, and he was a member of FGV's entrepreneurship league (2023 to 2024). His profile describes Kayro as helping industries, distributors and wholesalers sell more volume and a better mix with AI built into WhatsApp. Paulo Chade worked on AI deployment and then product at Enter (2025 to April 2026) and did internships at Ant Group (credit-scoring models, 2024) and BTG Pactual (blockchain, 2022). João Henrique Santos was a software engineer at Segura (2024 to July 2026) and, from 2023 to 2025, a course assistant at Harvard University (CS50, Math 1A and Math 21b). Their profiles date the Kayro roles to April 2026 (Antonio and Paulo) and August 2026 (João). The business runs through a Brazilian company, Datacado Ltda, opened in September 2025 with Antonio and Paulo as administrators; a US company called Kayro, LLC became one of its partners on 2026-08-07. Harvard may be what connects the founders, but only João's profile shows a Harvard role, so this is a lead and not a finding. The site names no customers, revenue or funding, and no press coverage of Kayro was found, so the story after the founding is unknown.

value: Cartsy is a consumer shopping assistant for people who 'shop with their eyes'. The user follows the account @cartsyapp on Instagram and sends it any post, reel or story, as they would to a friend; photos, screenshots and plain text also work. Cartsy reads the video or image, spots each item and searches real stores across the web, then replies with the matching products and prices and a link straight to the retailer, where the user buys at the store's price. The same account works in a web app at cartsy.com and in an iOS app, with one history, one collection of saved finds and one cart shared across Instagram and the web: products, posts and uploads are kept and searchable, users can bookmark products, build collections (gift ideas, outfits) and compare offers from several stores. It answers in English, Portuguese and Spanish. The service is free: users pay only for what they buy at the store, and the privacy policy says that a Cartsy-managed checkout may be offered (with a payment processor holding the card data), so revenue probably comes from retailer commissions or checkout, though the site does not say. The product belongs to CR AI Labs, Inc. and the landing page shows 'Backed by' the logo of Speedrun; a16z speedrun's own company page confirms that Cartsy is in its seventh residency cohort (SR007), is based in New York and has a team of three. That page, written by the company, describes it as the agentic-commerce layer for social media, aimed at what it calls the US$120 billion social-commerce market (the company's own figure), turning content into something shoppable in seconds with multimodal language models and a product-matching engine of its own, either as a creator's link-in-bio storefront or as an AI shopping agent that people use inside Instagram or TikTok. The founders are Alain Michel, CEO, a Brazilian entrepreneur with a Duke economics degree who founded the pet-products company Mundo Pet (sold to Cobasi, according to his speedrun profile), co-founded Lastro and was COO of BR Media Group; and Raul Dagir, founder and chief product officer, a Stanford graduate and hardware engineer who worked at Two Sigma and co-founded drachma before this. Their LinkedIn profiles, read through Linked API, show them in a stealth company from September 2025 and January 2026. In Brazil every investment fund needs an administrator that handles registration of investors, quota accounting, regulatory filings, custody relationships and the reports sent to investors; for private equity and venture funds (FIPs) and receivables funds (FIDCs) this work has long been done with spreadsheets, e-mail and paper. value: Problem: Brazil's structured-fund industry has grown fast but the back office has not. FIPs and FIDCs are run by managers who depend on administrators that handle investor registration, capital calls, quota accounting and filings through e-mail and spreadsheets, and the investors (including new retail and qualified ones) expect the experience of a digital bank. Logic: since CVM Resolution 175 and the rise of private credit, thousands of fund classes need an administrator, and a software-first administrator can serve each one at lower cost and with better data than a bank-owned one; it also earns a recurring fee on assets that tend to stay in closed funds for years. Market: ANBIMA reports that FIDCs held R$741 billion in net assets in November 2025, with about 3,800 fund classes and 426 managers, and that FIPs and FIDCs raised R$60.1 billion and R$57.6 billion net in 2025, the largest inflows after fixed income. Our rough estimate of the revenue pool: administration plus custody and bookkeeping fees of perhaps 0.05% to 0.15% of assets (our assumption, not a sourced figure) on FIDC assets alone gives R$0.4 billion to R$1.1 billion a year; adding FIPs, FICs and FIFs makes the pool meaningfully larger. If Nash won 3% to 5% of fund assets in a decade, that is on the order of R$10 million to R$50 million of annual revenue; this is a range from our arithmetic, not a forecast. Different: the founders come from fund administration (Apex, Vórtx), fund law and fund software (Softpar), and the company is building its own regulated entity rather than selling software to incumbents, which is harder but gives control of the experience. Fit with Norte: the Manifesto says Norte backs obsessed founders, does not meddle with operations and adds value by connecting people and bringing top funds to cap tables; a regulated administrator needs exactly that, since its customers are fund managers, many of them in Norte's network of 400+ operators and investors. This is our reading, not a statement by Norte. Risks: the licence path is long and partly pending (the DTVM licence was not granted when the site was read); incumbents (Vórtx, Apex, Oliveira Trust, BTG and Itaú units) compete on price and trust; and administration revenue is small per fund, so the business needs scale and a clean regulatory record. The company is also very young, with no public customer or asset figures.

value: Strattum is a Brazilian startup that builds the layer between a large company's scattered data and its artificial-intelligence tools. Most big firms keep information in ERPs, CRMs, data lakes, spreadsheets and documents; when they connect a CRM directly to a language model, the answers are poor and the token bill is high. Strattum does not build agents or models of its own. It connects those sources once, organises and relates the information, and keeps it in a governed 'context layer', which it calls the company brain, so that different models and agents can reuse the same context with fewer tokens and cheaper models. It stresses four benefits for large enterprises: faster AI projects, lower operating cost, data sovereignty (the technology runs in the customer's own environment) and information governance with access controls. It sells across industries (retail, finance, technology and the real economy) with a first focus on financial services and on Brazil. Revenue comes from a hybrid model: a fixed platform subscription that includes a token allowance, plus a transactional fee above it; dedicated forward-deployed engineers help each customer start, though the company says it does not aim to profit from that service. The company was founded in early 2026 by Carlos Eduardo 'Kadu' Monguilhott, CEO, who spent 11 years at Neoway, including as CEO, and took part in its sale to B3 in 2021 (R$1.8 billion, per Mixvale), and Rafael Viana, CTO, co-founder of the identity-verification company Certta, where they met. In June 2026 it announced a US$3.2 million pre-seed co-led by Maya Capital and ONEVC with Norte Ventures and three angels, among them Andrew Prozes (former CEO of LexisNexis) and Jim Peck (former CEO of TransUnion, now at NielsenIQ). It said it already had initial customers with high tickets for the stage and planned 35 hires by the end of 2026, including people from QuintoAndar, Red Hat and Neoway. By late July it had begun testing the platform abroad and was weighing a new round for international expansion, with an ambition to become a Brazilian big tech. On 2026-09-09 it acquired Tropicalia, a Silicon Valley context-engineering start-up founded in 2025, in an acqui-hire: Tropicalia ceased operating and its founders Arthur Guttilla (head of product marketing and partnerships) and Leonardo Miranda (application team) joined Strattum. Next steps named: connecting the company brain to more enterprise customers, advancing governance and putting more use cases in production on cheaper models.

value: Fina is a Venezuelan software company that sells a cloud administrative system to small and medium businesses and is now adding credit on top of it. The product replaces the notebook, the Excel file and the phone notes with one platform for sales, inventory, accounts receivable and payable, bank accounts, customers and profit reports, working in bolivars and dollars at the same time: it takes the Central Bank of Venezuela's rate, computes the exchange difference and lets the same invoice be issued in bolivars, dollars or euros. It is built for poor connectivity and power cuts, and runs from a phone. Customers are bodegas, hardware and auto-parts shops, clothing and tech stores, restaurants, barbershops and distributors. The subscription starts at about US$35 a month (Bloomberg Línea, at the official rate) and includes invoicing, inventory and a basic CRM; the company says its customers asked, before Fina, for nothing more than Excel or a notebook (about 90% according to a co-founder), so the real competitor is having no system at all, and that foreign tools such as QuickBooks do not handle several currencies in one account. The company also ships AI features: stock is loaded from a photo of the supplier invoice, and Nina, an agent trained on the business's own sales, costs and cash flow, answers questions such as what to restock. The founders are four Venezuelans: Enrique Rivas (CEO), Diego Aponte, Alejandro Fariña (CTO) and Sebastián Sánchez. Rivas and Aponte had started, in their teens, Caracas Ron, a liquor delivery business, and an imported-goods shop; the cash that did not match, the inventory that vanished and three administrative systems that did not fit Venezuelan trade led them to build their own. Fina reached the market at the end of 2023. Its second line is Fina Presta, a loan for businesses that have used Fina for at least 60 days: US$100 to US$3,000, no collateral or paperwork, requested inside the platform, paid out in bolivars in under 30 minutes and repaid in fortnightly instalments, with a line that grows as the business pays on time; the pilot users spent 85% of the money on stock. The lender uses the sales and inventory history Fina already holds as its credit data. In August 2026 Fina announced a US$1 million seed round co-led by SquareOne Capital and Tomorrow Capital, with Norte Ventures, Platanus and Neer Venture Partners and Latin American SaaS and fintech angels (Omie, Bold, Conta Simples, Colektia, Hackmetrix). It followed two smaller earlier rounds of US$100,000 and US$350,000 (Startup Researcher, undated). The company reports more than 5,000 active businesses, close to US$2 million in annual recurring revenue and about 50 new customers a day, and says Fina Presta grows 2x month over month. The money is for financial products and AI tools over six months, digital invoicing, automatic financial statements that could become an auditable credit history, and, longer term, expansion across Latin America with a goal of US$10 to 20 million ARR.

Logic: a very low-cost subscription (about US$35 a month) wins the daily record of sales, stock and cash; that record is then the only credit data the business has, so lending to the same customers is cheaper to underwrite and safer than any outside lender can manage. Why now: electronic invoicing rules from the tax authority (SENIAT) make a system an obligation, and since January 2026 the country moved from excluded to a market foreign investors are looking at (LatAm Fintech), with the UNDP projecting 2026 growth of 7.4% and inflation near 272%, so many businesses need tools to see their numbers before investing. Market: no recent official count of Venezuelan SMEs was readable. The only figure read is a Fedecámaras president's 2018 statement of about 280,000 companies, down from more than 490,000 twenty years earlier (Panamá América, EFE), which is old and probably lower today; our assumption is 150,000 to 250,000 formal businesses that could use such a system. Bottom-up: 5,000 customers at US$35 a month is US$2.1 million a year, which matches the US$2 million ARR the company reports; 100,000 customers (the CTO's multi-year ambition) would be about US$42 million a year in subscriptions; at the assumed 150,000 to 250,000 businesses, the whole subscription market is roughly US$60 to 100 million a year at this price, so a strong outcome is a 30% to 50% share, around US$20 to 50 million, and lending revenue (loans of US$100 to US$3,000 repeated through the year) can add as much again if credit losses are controlled. Beyond Venezuela the company says it wants to reach other emerging markets, which is a stated aim, not evidence. What is different: it is designed for dollarised, two-currency commerce and low connectivity, sells to the business that has no system at all rather than displacing a rival, and has a lending product that uses its own data. Comparables named in the sources and read: Omie (Brazil) and Bold (Colombia), whose founders invested as angels, built administrative or payments platforms for small businesses in unstable economies; Cashea (Venezuela, US$100 million raised in 2026 per Bloomberg Línea) shows investor appetite for Venezuelan fintech. value: KHAL is a Brazilian platform for building and running AI agents in the customer-service, sales and retention operations of large companies. It is made by Namastex Labs (legal name Namastex Labs Serviços em Tecnologia Ltda, trade name KHAL), a generative-AI research lab from Uberlândia, Minas Gerais. The pitch is that CX teams are 'held hostage by their own software': KHAL takes a company's knowledge base, rules and past conversations, maps conflicts and duplicates between them, and puts agents in production across chat, voice and WhatsApp, with the service, sales and retention context kept in one place so that the customer never retells the story. The company says the first agent is live in two weeks and sells through forward-deployed engineers who work inside each client in squads (the careers page lists senior and mid-level FDEs, a knowledge-base ETL owner and customer-success and enterprise-sales leads). It also runs AI CX Brasil, a media and research arm with a news radar, guides, columns and studies, and a free 'IAzômetro' diagnostic of how mature a company's use of AI in service is.Namastex Labs was founded in 2022 (the company says in the second half of the year, three months before ChatGPT; the registry opens it on 2022-04-26) as a research lab in Uberlândia with Felipe Rosa as the administrator since day one. In 2023 and 2024 it contributed to the open-source Langflow project and released its own tools, among them Genie, with thousands of weekly downloads, and its first enterprise work came from outside Brazil. In 2025 a merger with an AI-native edtech gave it product vision and knowledge of the CX market, and KHAL took shape as an agentic platform for enterprise CX. Antonio Gouveia, who the company calls KHAL's founder and who has been an administrator of the legal entity since April 2026. Customers named are Hapvida, Callink and Movecta. For Hapvida, a large Brazilian health-insurance group, KHAL built Eugênia, a sales agent that went live 13 days after the decision to start (17 April 2026), is connected to 16 legacy systems, talks by text, voice and image, and in six months served more than 400,000 people, of whom more than 13,000 bought a plan (27,000 lives); the company says leads that passed through it convert three times more. For Movecta it reads support tickets, fills more than ten Salesforce fields and routes the case with about 90% accuracy and almost no human validation. All of these figures are the company's. In September 2026 KHAL ran a stand at CONAREC and collected 1,035 survey answers from 478 companies; in October 2026 it hired Tarcísio Gotto (15 years at Zup, the last as CTO) to lead technology and Riemann Cesar (more than 25 years in Contax, AlmaViva and Algar) to lead revenue. In August 2026 a US entity, Namastex Labs LLC, became a partner of the Brazilian company, and the company says it is expanding go-to-market outside Brazil. No funding round was found in readable sources.
