value: Problem: large Brazilian consumer-facing companies (health insurers, banks, telecoms, retailers) run service and sales contact centres with thousands of agents, fragmented legacy systems and strict regulation, and their chatbots were rule-based and failed at anything not scripted; each unresolved contact costs money and each missed lead is lost revenue. Logic: language models now make it possible for an agent to read policies and past conversations, query internal systems and finish a task, so the contact centre can be partly replaced and, more importantly, can start selling and retaining; the company's Hapvida case (live in 13 days, 400,000 people served in six months, 13,000 plans sold, three times the conversion of leads that did not pass through the agent, all company figures) is the kind of proof large buyers need to repeat the project in other journeys, and KHAL's model of engineers embedded in each client turns one project into expansion. Why now: LLM agents became reliable enough in 2025 and 2026, and Brazilian service is heavily outsourced and labour-based. Market: the only independent size read is the consultancy E-Consulting's estimate that Brazil's contact-center market, outsourced and in-house, billed R$54.1 billion in 2019 (R$51.3 billion in 2018; TI Inside), which is old, so we treat it as an order of magnitude of about R$50 to 70 billion a year today (our assumption, not a source). If AI agents captured 10% to 20% of that spend, the pool is R$5 to 14 billion a year (about US$1 to 2.5 billion at roughly R$5.5 a dollar); a vendor that took 5% to 10% of that pool would bill about R$250 million to R$1.4 billion (US$50 to 250 million). Latin America and other countries are an upside the company states as its plan, not evidence. What is different: it starts from a research lab with open-source credibility (Langflow, Genie), sells outcomes to enterprises rather than a self-serve tool, ships fast, and has hired leaders from Zup and the outsourcing industry who know its buyers. Competitors are global agent platforms (Sierra, Decagon and Netomi were named as raising money in CX funding roundups in the search results; those pages were not read), Brazilian conversational vendors and the BPOs themselves, which will also sell AI. Fit with Norte: our reading, not Norte's statement. Norte says it backs highly intelligent, obsessed founders, builds on its network of operators and does not meddle in operations; KHAL's team came out of research and sells to large companies, where an operator network can open doors and help hire senior go-to-market talent, as the October 2026 hires suggest the company needs. Risks: crowded category where foundation-model providers and global platforms can undercut; enterprise concentration (Hapvida is the reference); long sales cycles; the services-heavy, FDE-based delivery limits margins and speed; and little public information (no round, price or revenue found). Confidence is low: the market size is old and every traction number is the company's.

value: Manor presents itself as an AI layer of tax intelligence for Brazilian companies. Its starting point is that following Brazilian tax rules alongside a company's operation is humanly impossible: the site cites IBPT for the number of new tax laws published every day, plus dozens of decisions, and the tax reform runs until 2033 (2026 is a test year with CBS at 0.9% and IBS at 0.1%; PIS, COFINS and IPI are phased out and ICMS and ISS fall to 90%, 80%, 70% and 60% of today's rates while IBS rises). Manor reads laws and decisions daily from federal, state and municipal sources and from STF, STJ, TRFs, state courts, CARF and the Receita Federal, summarises them with filters by source, tax and theme, connects them to each customer's operation, flags risks (a divergent tax classification, for instance) before they become problems, keeps the customer's tax matrix up to date with the official source beside each change, and organises the grounds to decide whether to keep, adjust or contest. It also compares current law with the reform. It sells in four ways: a corporate plan for the tax and finance teams that answer for taxes; a partnership for accounting firms, so they can offer clients new, higher-value services; a partnership for law firms, with research on official sources and changes affecting each client; and an individual subscription, a basic tax-research copilot with official sources, with 30% off under approval and partnerships with the OAB (the site's wording). The founder is Rodrigo Salvador, a repeat entrepreneur from Rio de Janeiro. He started the student network Passei Direto in 2012, at 22, with a co-founder (Brazil Journal names André Simões), and ran it as CEO; in March 2021 UOL Edtech bought 100% of it, mostly in cash, an exit for all its funds (Redpoint eventures, Valor Capital, Península, Crescera, Endeavor Catalyst and Chegg), and Salvador and his partner stayed on as UOL Edtech executives. His profile shows CEO of Passei Direto until January 2022 and then VP of Strategy, M&A and the B2B business unit at UOL. MIT Technology Review named him one of its Innovators Under 35 Latin America in 2022, and his profile also cites Forbes 30 Under 30 and Endeavor. Since October 2025 his profile lists him as co-founder of a 'Stealth Startup' under the headline 'Helping to build the future of tax'; it does not name Manor, so the link to Manor is our inference from the headline and from the registry, where he is the sole administrator of Manor Desenvolvimento de Software Ltda., opened on 2025-09-01 in Campinas with R$1.54 million of capital and a US company, Manor Tax LLC, as a partner from the first day. The owner's own reading of his profile suggests that other co-founders exist, but no readable page names them. The site names no team, customers, revenue or funding, and no press on Manor was found, so traction and funding are unknown.

value: Problem: Brazilian companies pay for one of the most complex tax systems in the world and are about to live through the biggest change in decades, the 2026 to 2033 transition to CBS and IBS with the old taxes running in parallel. Tax teams and accounting firms cannot read every new law and ruling, so they miss credits and take avoidable risks. Logic: language models can read and summarise legal text at low marginal cost, and a product that ties each change to a specific company's operation (not a generic news feed) turns tax into a daily, auditable routine; the reform gives a dated reason to buy now. Market (assumption, not data): Brazil has 101,880 registered accounting organisations (Escola Exchange benchmark, via Sitecontabil), and 79% of them have no structured commercial department, which says many are small and under pressure to find new services. If 2% of them (about 2,000) paid R$1,000 to R$3,000 a month, that is R$24M to R$72M a year from accountants alone; a corporate plan for mid-sized and large companies could be larger per customer, and law firms and individuals add a long tail. A strong outcome is the default tax-monitoring layer for Brazilian accounting firms and mid-market tax teams. What is different: daily monitoring that is linked to the customer's own operation and to the reform, an OAB partnership channel for lawyers and a partner channel through accountants who already own the customer relationship; and a founder who has already built and sold a Brazilian internet company. Fit with Norte (our reading): Rodrigo Salvador built Passei Direto from age 22 to a sale to UOL Edtech in 2021 and then worked inside a large group on strategy, M&A and B2B, so he is the kind of obsessed, proven founder the Manifesto describes; a vertical AI company that sells through accounting firms and enterprise tax teams is a place where a network of operators helps with introductions, hiring and first revenue. The owner reads many Norte connections in his profile; that is an observation we could not verify from a page. Norte's participation is not documented in any Source. Risks: established tax-content and compliance vendors and ERPs add similar AI features; wrong tax answers carry liability; the depth of the product and its customer base are not verifiable; the company is months old, and only one of its founders is known. Confidence is low.

value: Sempre+ is a Brazilian pediatric service that lives entirely inside WhatsApp. A parent sends a message, with no app to download and no sign-up, and the first reply comes from Dra. Med, a health assistant trained by the company's medical team that listens to the case, explains first care, what signs to watch and when to seek a doctor or the emergency room. That conversation is free and unlimited, any hour of the day. When a case needs a diagnosis, prescription or treatment, Dra. Med hands it to a pediatrician registered with the CRM, who continues in the same chat by text or by video. Each consultation is paid on its own, with no subscription or lock-in: the company's machine-readable page lists R$27 for a text consultation and R$43 for video. Prescriptions and certificates are issued during the consultation when needed. The medical team is published with name, CRM number and training hospital (Sírio-Libanês, Albert Einstein, HC-FMUSP and São Paulo's public health system), the technical responsible is Dra. Nicole Micheloni, and the service says it follows Brazil's telemedicine rules (CFM Resolution 2,314/2022) and the LGPD. It serves children and adolescents from 0 to 18, always with a legal guardian starting the conversation, and is explicit that it is not an emergency service. The idea, as the company tells it, is that almost every parent's doubt about a child's health arises outside office hours, when the choice is between waiting in fear and a night in the emergency room. The founders are two operators who worked together at the Belo Horizonte edtech Trybe. Bruna Keiserman, founder and CEO, started on Sempre+ in October 2025; her profile shows ex-Amazon and ex-BCG in the headline, then Chief of Staff to the CEO (2021) and COO (2022 to March 2024) of Trybe, running a 200-person operations team, an Entrepreneur-in-Residence stint at the venture firm Atlântico in 2024 to develop her next venture, COO of BrandLovrs from November 2024 to February 2025, and an earlier food-delivery startup, Mimic, which she founded in 2019. Gabriela Migliorini, co-founder and chief product and technology officer, joined in January 2026 after being Head of Product for Jus IA at Jusbrasil in 2025; before that she was one of Trybe's first employees (number 20), as Head of Data from 2019 and then Head of Product, and she studied computer engineering with research and data roles in France and at Michelin. value: Problem: parents of young children have urgent but usually minor questions at night and on weekends, and the usual answers are an emergency room, an unreliable internet search or a wait for an appointment. Logic: WhatsApp is the channel Brazilians already use for everything, telemedicine has been legal since 2022 (CFM Resolution 2,314/2022, per the company's own pages), and language models make a free first-line assistant cheap enough that only cases needing a doctor cost money. A free triage that converts to pay-per-consult at R$27 to R$43 is also an easy trial for a family without health insurance. Market: Brazil's population under 18 is on the order of 50 million (our approximation of IBGE Census data, not verified from a page we read), in perhaps 25 million households (our assumption). If 5% of those households became regular users who pay for three consultations a year at about R$35, the pool is about 1.25 million families x 3 x R$35, roughly R$130 million a year; a range of R$50 million to R$400 million covers 2% to 8% adoption and two to four consultations. A share of 5% to 10% of that pool would be R$7 million to R$40 million of yearly revenue, before any subscription, employer or insurer channel. Different: it is WhatsApp-native with no app, starts free with an assistant, and publishes its doctors' CRM numbers; other WhatsApp pediatric services exist (a search turned up Usawa Care in Portugal), so the idea itself is not unique and the edge has to come from execution. Fit with Norte (our reading): the founders come from Trybe, a company in Norte's own portfolio, where Bruna Keiserman was COO and Gabriela Migliorini an early employee and Head of Product, so they are operators a Norte network already knows; the Manifesto says Norte backs obsessed founders at an early stage, does not meddle with operations and adds value by connecting people, hiring and revenue from day zero, which fits a consumer health start-up that needs doctors, health-plan buyers and consumer-growth operators. The venture firm Valutia, whose portfolio page also lists Caveo, Nomo, Datamint and Refer, all in Norte's portfolio, backs the company; whether Norte took part is unknown, and no Round is recorded. Risks: quality and liability in remote pediatric care, regulatory limits on AI and telemedicine (the company's own terms cite a 2026 CFM resolution), high acquisition costs for a pay-per-use consumer product, and no evidence yet of repeat use or margins. The company opened in March 2026, so almost everything is untested.

Logic: models are now good enough to act through e-mail, calendar and CRM connectors, so a firm that packages agents, integrations and deployment as a service can go live in days and learn from many customers. Market: no market-size page was read. Our rough estimate: Brazil has on the order of 100,000 firms with enough staff to buy an agent service (our assumption); at R$60,000 to R$300,000 a year each (our assumption) the pool is R$6 billion to R$30 billion, and a realistic 1% to 3% reached in five years would be R$60 million to R$900 million, a very wide range because we know neither the customer segment nor the price. Different: nothing in the product is visible yet beyond speed to deploy and a Rio base; agent-as-a-service is crowded (model labs, automation vendors and many Brazilian start-ups listed in directories such as Mapa IA Brasil). What is distinctive is the team and its position: two former investors, one a programmer by training, who sit at the centre of the Claude community in Rio (a Claude Community Ambassador host and sponsors of local events), which is a channel to the first customers and to talent. Fit with Norte (our reading): the Manifesto says Norte backs obsessed founders and helps with hiring, revenue from day zero and bringing funds onto cap tables; founders with ten years of investing behind them know the cap-table side already, and an applied-AI services company needs customers and talent more than capital, which is where a connector is useful. This is our reading only; Norte's participation is not documented. Risks: commoditisation by model providers, services-like margins, dependence on a single model vendor (the site says it is powered by Claude), and almost no public evidence of customers or traction, so the case rests on the founders; both come from finance and neither has run a software company that we could verify.
